articles.title: Anthropic CEO sells investors on safety, 'no jerks' culture
articles.summary: Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei pitched investors on safety and a strict hiring culture on Friday, days before the AI company's stock market debut.Nvi...
articles.body:
Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei pitched investors on safety and a strict hiring culture on Friday, days before the AI company's stock market debut.

"We're very paranoid" about AI safety, Amodei told JPMorgan Chase chief Jamie Dimon at an event hosted by the bank, one of the offering's lead underwriters.

He said that focus had shaped both Anthropic's culture and its strategy, steering it toward business customers and coding tools rather than consumer chatbots, a path not initially chosen by the company's archrival ChatGPT-maker OpenAI.

"We deliberately chose enterprise as a focus because we understood that it was synergistic with our focus on safety," he said.

The listing comes at a sensitive moment for the AI boom. AI stocks have swung sharply as investors question whether heavy spending on the technology will pay off.

Nvidia, the chip giant at the center of the AI buildout and an Anthropic investor, has been rocked by the resignation of chief executive Jensen Huang after he admitted to an affair with a woman US intelligence reportedly believes was a Chinese spy.

Anthropic set a price range this week of $70 to $78 per share, with the stock, under the ticker name "ANT," expected to beginning trading on Thursday.

At the top of that range, the offering would raise up to $64.4 billion and value the company at about $1.4 trillion, including employee stock options and restricted shares. That is well below the $2 trillion figure floated earlier in the year.

Amodei, who has a doctorate in biology, co-founded Anthropic in 2021 after leaving OpenAI. He told investors the company would keep opening new markets by pushing the limits of its technology.

"AI isn't just one application; it isn't just one market," he said. "You're on an exponential of cognition, and as the exponential proceeds, new markets become possible."

He predicted that fields such as scientific research would be "much larger than coding, in the same way that coding was much larger than chatbots."

Yet "Anthropic tends to under promise and over deliver. We're not going to go out and say we're going to solve this problem and that problem and that problem."

Amodei said he spends "probably 40, 50 percent" of his time on talent and culture, which he called "the most important things."

Every hire goes through a culture interview, he said, and the company has turned down technically gifted candidates who did not fit.

"We don't want people who are jerks. We don't want people who try to steal the show and don't work well with others," he said. "We don't want people who aren't oriented towards the public benefit."

articles.title: Anthropic IPO Buyers Have More Influence on Price Than SpaceX
articles.summary: Anthropic PBC will try next week to take SpaceX’s title of the biggest public listing of all time, but unlike Elon Musk’s conglomerate, major investors will...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- Anthropic PBC will try next week to take SpaceX's title of the biggest public listing of all time, but unlike Elon Musk's conglomerate, major investors will have more sway on its initial share price at a time when the artificial-intelligence trade is in flux.

The Claude developer is gauging interest in its shares at a range of $70 to $78 for its initial public offering, a departure from SpaceX, which used a take-it-or-leave-it approach by setting a fixed price of $135 a share in the marketing phase.

And while Anthropic wants the bragging rights of having the biggest IPO ever, some market watchers are warning that it shouldn't be too aggressive on pricing so institutional investors will feel like they got a fair price and shares will have room to rise on day one.

"Anthropic is doing a more conventional roadshow and when you set the IPO price based on institutional demand that makes it less likely to trade below the IPO," said Harrison Rolfes, a senior research analyst for late-stage company research at Pitchbook.

But there are no guarantees. A challenging market backdrop — including the ouster of Jensen Huang at Nvidia Corp. — has made final stages of Anthropic's march to public markets more complicated than SpaceX's $86.2 billion listing in June.

SpaceX, whose shares now trade 3% above its IPO price, benefited from coming to market in a quarter in which the Nasdaq 100 Index jumped nearly 28%. The same index is down about 7% in the last three months after a US interest-rate hike, widespread worries about an oversupply of AI debt and a midterm election result where the data centers that power models like ChatGPT and Claude drew the ire of voters. Those factors have hushed earlier whispers about Anthropic having a $2 trillion valuation.

"It seems like they really are listening to the market," said Andy Tang, a partner at venture capital firm Draper Associates and a former technology investment banker. "They are bringing the IPO at a more conservative level."

Anthropic is now targeting a fully diluted valuation of about $1.4 trillion. It plans to raise as much as $64.4 billion in the IPO and $26 billion in a private placement, a total that would surpass SpaceX's IPO.

articles.title: Jensen Huang’s departure blasts big hole in AI startup funding, VCs and founders say
articles.summary: Nvidia poured tens of billions into AI startups under Huang. Without him at the helm, founders and VCs are bracing for smaller checks and lower valuations.
articles.body:
It was the resignation heard across the world. Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s embattled CEO who co-founded and led the company for 33 years, had officially stepped down . “It’s like a bomb went off,” one neocloud founder told TechCrunch when he first heard the news.

Over the last several years, Nvidia has been a prolific investor , pouring tens of billions into startups annually and participating in 105 rounds this year alone, often as the largest investor, according to PitchBook. “If that direction changes, it’ll be a big blow to so many young companies,” said Maria Davidson, founder of Relational Capital.

Huang’s absence leaves the startup ecosystem without one of its biggest champions and with far less capital for now, investors say, which could have a massive impact on dealmaking, valuations, funding, and even competition.

“Nvidia is carrying almost every AI-native startup from application to neocloud,” Dawn Capital’s Shamillah Bankiya told TechCrunch.

Most of the significant decisions to invest in startups often came from Jensen himself, according to Umesh Padval, managing partner at Seligman Ventures. Padval has known Huang since serving on the board of Mellanox Technologies, a networking chipmaker Nvidia acquired for approximately $7 billion in 2020. While there is hope that Huang’s eventual successor will resume his dealmaking spree, investors aren’t hopeful that it will happen in the short term.

Nvidia’s interim CEO, Colette Kress, is expected to institute some changes , especially when it comes to Nvidia’s investments into AI startups at the crux of the billion-dollar data center build-out . Huang’s rampant dealmaking in this sphere has been a source of concern for Wall Street.

“She’s much more conservative,” one investor said of Kress. “I don’t think she’s going to commit the same amount of money to keep the early-stage ecosystem going.”

Nvidia’s biggest bets were backing neoclouds, inference providers, and open weight models, which are expensive for smaller companies to build. “Jensen’s initiatives are a big reason an ecosystem has emerged despite that,” Zain Javaid, co-founder of the hardware company Ghost, said.

For instance, Nvidia backed CoreWeave when it was still private and participated in two of Crusoe’s rounds, including its $1.4 billion Series E. It bought Hugging Face this year for $13 billion (expected to close in 2027) and holds investments in Mistral AI, Lambda, and Black Forest Labs. Nvidia was often the largest investor in the deals. Last year, it wrote an $800 million check into a $2 billion Series B round for Reflection AI, before the open source startup began to earn meaningful revenue, according to the Wall Street Journal .

“Jensen believed in open source and frankly speaking, Europe,” Bankiya said of how Huang invested so much in AI across the world. The cease of that support in other regions outside of America, like Europe “would be a massive funding and honestly ecosystem gap that no one can fill.”

It’s also true that Nvidia was such a dominant player in the ecosystem that at times, it felt like a monopoly. By backing so many companies with such generous checks, Nvidia effectively locked those startups into using its chips, which helped reinforce its dominant market position.

If the company does grow more conservative with its startup investments, that could leave more room for rivals and smaller competitors. (Coincidentally, Google announced two new chips this week amid Huang’s Nvidia fallout.)

Some investors with whom TechCrunch spoke hope that large cloud companies and other chipmakers will step in to back startups and fill some of the void that will likely be left by Huang.

Dharmesh Thakker, a general partner at Battery Ventures, for example, expects Big Tech rivals to vie for Nvidia’s investment crown, “depending upon who brings the best combination of a great product, an ecosystem and community to compete with CUDA, and the financial power to bankroll the ecosystem,” he said. CUDA is Nvidia’s software platform that enables developers to run AI models on its GPUs.

While companies like Google, Amazon, Microsoft, and AMD may back mature startups to drive adoption of their chips and clouds, Thakker doubts they will pour hundreds of millions into pre-revenue infrastructure startups the way Nvidia did.

Under Huang, infrastructure companies that needed $100 million to $500 million in GPUs would often raise half of that amount at valuations of $1 billion or more from Nvidia just to get started, one VC said. The chipmaker’s participation gave other investors the comfort in backing these companies at the lofty valuations.

Now Nvidia is expected to be more selective in the new companies it backs, while writing smaller-sized checks into its existing portfolio, contributing to a drop in valuations.

“When Nvidia was on the cap table, everyone felt safe,” Padval said. Without that backing, investors say traditional VCs are likely to think twice before writing checks into these startups and may even pause certain dealmaking.

Even so, few believe that Nvidia’s investment slowdown will by itself halt the broader AI boom.

Though everyone agrees that Huang is a massive loss for Nvidia, one of his ex-employees, Amulya Vishwanath, who now runs her own VC fund, said that “founders and leaders must be held accountable,” and that the ecosystem is bigger than one person. “That talent will, and must, continue to thrive.”

articles.title: Amazon has a plan to index the world’s online shopping data
articles.summary: Amazon reportedly has a plan for a World Product Graph that would compile data on products across the internet.
articles.body: Amazon has plans to build a vault of data on every product sold anywhere on the internet, even products Amazon doesn’t sell, and make the information available through its own site, according to Reuters. The project, called the “World Product Graph,” is meant to make it less likely that shoppers leave Amazon to do their product research on Reddit or Google, and make it more likely shoppers end up at Amazon even if they’re searching for a product sold elsewhere. The same goes for AI agents — if Amazon has the largest stockpile of shopping data, AI agents may rely on its index of products over others, so even people shopping with bots will end up on its pages. Links to outside retailers’ products have already started popping up on Amazon through the “shop direct” feature it launched last year. The company also has its own AI shopping assistant, Alexa for Shopping, previously called Rufus. The World Product Graph project would also be aimed at fixing issues with the AI by providing it more data. According to Reuters, an internal Amazon document on the project says “Many Rufus answers are factually wrong or incomplete” and running users’ Amazon searches with the AI is expensive. Adding more data is reportedly supposed to make the system more accurate and able to use cheaper models. Whether this actually ships is still up in the air. The internal document reportedly says the project “depends on discovering how brands organize their products on their own websites,” which could involve Amazon crawling other retailers’ sites. Reuters says it’s unclear “if or when this plan may be implemented,” but said the document on it included an October 1st, 2027 release date. Amazon said in a statement to Reuters that “Draft, outdated documents often paint an incomplete picture and the existence of a brainstorming document such as this one doesn’t necessarily reflect our current plans.”

articles.title: Tesla Starts Taking Cybercab Orders From Select Customers
articles.summary: Tesla Inc. invited select customers to place orders for the Cybercab in a step toward trying to make its driverless car available to consumers.
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- Tesla Inc. invited select customers to place orders for the Cybercab in a step toward trying to make its driverless car available to consumers.

The two-seat vehicle, which lacks a steering wheel and foot pedals, initially launched as part of Tesla's robotaxi service in Austin. Now, the Cybercab will be available via limited release in supported service areas, the company announced Friday on X.

The Cybercab will work unsupervised in all the same locations as Tesla's robotaxi fleet, Ashok Elluswamy, Tesla's head of artificial intelligence, said in a separate post on X. The company had previously posted an interest form for fleet operators, but not for individual owners.

Matt Holm, president of the Tesla Austin's Owners Club, posted screenshots of an email showing he ordered the vehicle after he was invited to reserve a Cybercab for $29,990, plus a $299 monthly subscription required to operate the vehicle.

It's unclear whether regulators would stand in the way of Tesla delivering driverless cars to consumers. One day after the car debuted in September, the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration opened a probe into the process and technical data Tesla relied on when the company self-certified the vehicles as compliant with all federal safety standards.

(Updates with detail from executive in the third paragraph.)

articles.title: Jensen Huang and the decline of the visionary showman founder CEO
articles.summary: Nvidia’s CEO was the last visionary Big Tech founder. What will the company do without him?
articles.body: On January 6th, 2025, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang got his rockstar moment at last. He strode triumphantly onstage, hand raised in the air, to the claps and cheers of a 14,000-person arena absolutely packed with influencers and fans, their faces awash in blue glow, as he made his entrance in a black leather jacket that shimmered in the stadium’s lights. Few are cheering for Jensen Huang now. He has left Nvidia after seemingly enabling two chip smuggling scandals and allegedly having three extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy at the same time he was mingling with President Donald Trump. The world is watching to see if this scandal might disrupt the entire US AI industry and perhaps destabilize the stock market along with it. That’s because Huang wasn’t merely running the first $5 trillion company, he was the visionary leader in control of the must-have GPUs powering the worldwide AI boom, part of a company that represents around 6 percent of the S&P 500 stock market index all by itself. And he didn’t plan for succession if he ever stepped down. The 63-year-old once said he preferred to die on the job; he once suggested he’d work until he was 90 or 100, then carry on leading the company as a robot. It’s not easy to replace Huang, partly because he had no deputies. Around 60 employees reported directly to the CEO. “He built the company around himself, and everything that happened there flowed through him,” says IDC analyst and former computing journalist Tom Mainelli. “Jensen is Nvidia, and Nvidia is Jensen,” Jon Peddie, a computer industry analyst who’s been tracking Nvidia since its inception, tells me. But Nvidia isn’t Jensen anymore. He has left the company he cofounded 33 years ago. It’s the end of an era, and not just for Nvidia — because Jensen Huang was Big Tech’s last true example of a visionary showman founder CEO. “He was both the visionary and the tactical leader, the closest thing tech has had to Steve Jobs,” Moor Insights & Strategy chief analyst Pat Moorhead tells me. Elon Musk didn’t exactly found Tesla and has quite the track record of broken promises, and Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg has proven to be neither visionary nor showman so far. Google’s Larry Page and Sergey Brin stepped away in 2019 as their company dealt with growing employee turmoil, leaving the company in the hands of Sundar Pichai, and both Microsoft and Apple have each passed the torch twice since the days of Bill Gates and Steve Jobs. Some say Apple’s Steve Jobs broke the CEO mold, but he created a mold of his own. Huang was one of countless tech leaders who followed his example by introducing their products in keynote speeches, adopting a single recognizable piece of clothing like Jobs’ trademark black turtleneck, and even occasionally teasing “one more thing” for the surprise at the end of their presentations. In the newsroom, we’d sometimes joke about the Jobs wannabes; many were stiff suits who didn’t have the credibility to pull it off. I thought Huang might be a Jobs wannabe, too, the first time I saw that he’d adopted a black jacket as his uniform. (It was not always a leather jacket; an earlier version was a Nvidia-branded softshell.) Huang later insisted on wearing a jacket even when the temperature was hot — more than once, I saw him sweat profusely rather than take it off. Unlike Jobs, he also held quite a few keynotes when he didn’t have much news to share; he liked to repeat the company’s previous accomplishments as if they were brand-new. But even if Huang didn’t have the same gravitas as Jobs, he did have exciting tech up his sleeves and loved to demo it onstage. He knew how to get people excited about the future of visual computing with eye-opening gaming graphics, physics and lighting demos, and eventually image recognition, AI weather simulations, digital copies of real-world factories, and the robots that can virtually train in them. His Nvidia tried to educate people about the how and why of GPUs, too; I still remember in 2008 when Nvidia invited the Mythbusters to demo the difference between serial processing and parallel processing by firing a 1,100-nozzle paintball gun to “paint” the Mona Lisa in one shot. [Media: What I didn’t know back then: Huang was a visionary founder. He took Nvidia to fame and fortune through a series of tremendous bets. In 1996, three years after he cofounded the company at a Denny’s diner, Nvidia nearly went out of business while working on a failed graphics chip for the Sega Dreamcast game console. But even though he didn’t deliver that chip, Huang personally convinced Sega to invest $5 million afterward, The Wall Street Journal reported in 2024. He then turned around and bet the company again on the Riva 128 PC graphics accelerator, an effort so ambitious he had to lay off over half of Nvidia’s roughly 100 staffers, skip the prototyping stage, and rush it straight to production, and he still only had one month of payroll left by the time it shipped, The New Yorker wrote in 2023. Thankfully, it was a success, selling a million units in just four months and paving the way for both the GeForce GPU and a long-term relationship with chip fabricator TSMC. Roughly eight years later, Huang decided it wasn’t enough to be the leader in PC gaming graphics alone. He bet the company’s entire gross profit, he told podcaster Lex Fridman, on shipping a new feature inside those graphics cards that no one had asked for: CUDA. It was the ability to use a GPU for other kinds of computing tasks beyond graphics, and Huang said it increased the cost of every GeForce graphics card by 50 percent. “Originally there was no market or market demand for it. It was almost as if they built it because they could,” says Peddie. “Jensen had the vision for what it could be and the courage to pursue it in spite of the opinions of others.” “NVIDIA was effectively investing in a computing platform that extended far beyond graphics, with no guarantee of a near-term return,” says HotTech analyst Dave Altavilla. “Huang saw that a GPU was really a parallel computer that happened to render graphics. CUDA turned that insight into a platform, and it’s why NVIDIA was ready when AI arrived,” Mainelli tells me. It was a bad time for graphics cards to suddenly cost more. When the Great Recession hit in 2007–2009, and Nvidia laptop graphics chips also started failing due to design defects, the company lost 80 percent of its market value. But Huang believed in CUDA enough to invest even more. “He literally handed out high-end NVIDIA GPUs to researchers at industry conferences, while the company seeded universities like Stanford with hardware to encourage development on its platform,” says Altavilla. And by 2012, Nvidia’s potential for AI had started to emerge. That’s when University of Toronto researchers used Nvidia GPUs to train a prize-winning image-recognition neural network called AlexNet, which is widely credited for sparking the AI revolution. Not all of Huang’s visions panned out the way he publicly expected. That AlexNet demo directly led to Huang’s bets on chips for self-driving cars, he said, but he didn’t exactly predict AI — CUDA was instead thought of as better and more affordable supercomputing for researchers and scientists. In 2013, I also wrote about how his grand plan for the future of the company relied heavily on putting Nvidia chips in your phone, which didn’t pan out. But that bet on ARM-based phone chips did put Nvidia inside every Nintendo Switch and may have helped make future “AI superchips” possible — the latest Nvidia AI server chips have ARM CPU cores. And in 2022, the leaders of the AI revolution launched the most groundbreaking AI tech yet on Nvidia hardware: ChatGPT. Six years earlier, Huang hand-delivered Nvidia’s first purpose-built AI workstation to OpenAI, and by 2022 Microsoft had strung together tens of thousands of Nvidia A100 GPUs to handle the load. [Image: [Image: “Every time competitors got close, he moved the fight up a level: the chip, then the server, then networking with the $6.9 billion Mellanox deal, then the full rack, all tied together by CUDA,” says Moorhead. “The speed came from how he ran the company,” he adds. “Decisions that took other companies four weeks took Nvidia four days.” As Nvidia’s fortunes and profit ballooned — thousands of dollars in pure profit every single second! — and as it became clearer that AI would reshape the world in one way or another, something strange happened. Huang became a celebrity. In summer 2024, The Wall Street Journal and social media chronicled that he received a hero’s welcome in his birthplace of Taiwan. He stopped over and over to sign autographs, including one on a woman’s chest. In person, at presentations, and in the company’s investor Q&As, I saw the tone shift. People began treating the leather-jacketed man like an actual rockstar instead of a wannabe rockstar, asking for photos and autographs and complimenting him rather than asking tough questions. It felt like he’d attained Steve Jobs’ infamous “reality distortion field” at last — until he popped that bubble himself with his infidelity. But one fewer reality distortion field in the world isn’t necessarily a bad thing, and as Apple has shown, a company doesn’t go bust just because its charismatic founder is gone. Tim Cook made Apple the most profitable company in the world. The question now is: who for Nvidia? “He was the king,” says Peddie. “Make no mistake – it was the Jensen Huang company. He called all the shots, took all the glory, and shouldered all the blame.” --- Does Nvidia work without Huang? Even without a named successor, analysts don’t think Nvidia is in big trouble yet. “This is a stock shock, not a business shock, for the next year. The roadmap and manufacturing are locked in through 2027,” says Pat Moorhead, Moor Insights & Strategy. “The question is whether Nvidia keeps inventing at Jensen’s pace once those plans run out. The bigger risk than any rival chip is customers hedging during a vacuum. That is why the next CEO needs technical credibility, an operating model that doesn’t depend on one person, and a plan to protect CUDA.” “Founder visionary, culture setter, leader, AI industry spokesperson etc., is the real loss. We don’t think anything changes strategically,” says Creative Strategies analyst Ben Bajarin.” The product roadmap is set and remains strong, and the next several generations are already in design, in tape-out or on order. NVIDIA is still the company best placed to ship its roadmap at scale, because it has spent years locking up the supply chain behind it, from leading-edge wafers and CoWoS-class packaging to HBM and the rack-level partners. That supply position does not walk out the door with one person.” “He was the consummate showman, salesman, and visionary for NVIDIA, so he will be hard to replace,” says IDC analyst Tom Mainelli. “But the company’s technology road map is sound, and the team behind him is still there. Choosing the right person to replace him will be key, and there will undoubtedly be bumps along the way. But the company will survive.” “Jensen built an exceptionally talented organization with a deep engineering bench, a mature, heavily-resourced software ecosystem, and strong customer relationships,” says Dave Altavilla, HotTech Vision and Analysis. “His departure undoubtedly leaves a leadership and strategic vision gap, but the technology, talent, and execution capabilities he helped establish aren’t going away. The real question is whether his successor can sustain that same long-term vision and willingness to invest ahead of the market.” “No one in the company really wants to step into his shoes, so an outsider is going to have to be found,” says Jon Peddie of Jon Peddie Research. “Whoever that is will not be Jensen, won’t have the same ambitions, the same contacts and relationships, the same vision, or the same courage to make big, long-term bets. We’ve seen this in Apple, AMD, Intel, and other companies. So the stock will probably get battered around a bit until investors see some stability and fewer ‘what if’ questions.”

articles.title: After blocking Chinese companies and their subsidiaries worldwide, Anthropic comes with another 'strict China ban'; tells companies in China and Hong Kong that you cannot ...
articles.summary: Institutional investors based in mainland China and Hong Kong have reportedly been shut out from placing orders in Anthropic PBC’s massive initial public
articles.body: Institutional investors based in mainland China and Hong Kong have reportedly been shut out from placing orders in Anthropic PBC’s massive initial public offering (IPO). According to a report by Bloomberg, Anthropic's 'IPO ban' highlights mounting geopolitical sensitivities surrounding the artificial intelligence industry. Citing people familiar with the matter, Bloomberg reported that several banks handling the offering have either refused to accept orders from buyers in those jurisdictions or deemed it unlikely they would receive share allocations. The restrictions stem in part from the US International Traffic in Arms Regulations (ITAR), which govern the trade of defense-related articles and services.San Francisco-based Anthropic and its co-founders are aiming to raise as much as $90.4 billion through the IPO and a concurrent private placement, targeting a $1.4 trillion valuation. According to deal terms reviewed by Bloomberg News, the offering is scheduled to price on November 18 and begin trading on the Nasdaq Global Select Market the following day under the ticker symbol ANT.Incidentally, Anthropic’s products are already unavailable in mainland China and Hong Kong, and earlier this year, the company blocked access for users traveling to those locations. Similarly in September 2025, Anthropic updated its service restriction policy to prohibit access from global subsidiaries of Chinese companies. In a statement published on its website, the San Francisco-based company laid out its updated terms of service, which now broaden access restrictions to entities “more than 50 per cent owned, directly or indirectly, by companies headquartered in unsupported regions”. “This update prohibits companies or organisations whose ownership structures subject them to control from jurisdictions where our products are not permitted, like China, regardless of where they operate,” it said.Anthropic is targeting a valuation of $1.25 trillion to $1.4 trillionDespite a sharp selloff in AI-related stocks last week, demand for the Claude chatbot maker’s debut remains intense, with prospective investors expressing interest for roughly six times the available shares. Some early backers have even begun offering portions of their IPO allocations to new buyers. According to a report in The Information, "Anthropic is targeting a valuation of $1.25 trillion to $1.4 trillion in its IPO next week, but some investors think that's too low. With its business already larger than OpenAI's, Anthropic could command an even higher price when shares begin trading."The exclusion mirrors the $86.2 billion IPO of Elon Musk’s Spacex earlier this year, during which international distribution coordinator Citigroup Inc. notified syndicate banks that Chinese and Hong Kong investors were barred under ITAR. In Anthropic's case, verbal guidance from the New York-based syndicate team similarly indicated that ITAR rules prohibit participation from the China region, though banks have not formally stopped sales teams from submitting client orders.How Anthropic IPO hints at the banIn its prospectus, Anthropic flagged escalating US-China tensions and heightened scrutiny from Washington regarding AI firms' exposure to Chinese state actors as key business risks. The company is also currently embroiled in a legal dispute with the Pentagon over a supply-chain risk designation, following an appeals court request last month by the Trump administration to reinstate a federal agency ban on Anthropic's technology.Your child uses AI every day. But do they understand it? Find out in the TOI AI Masterclass.

articles.title: The OpenAI board member who fired Sam Altman says we still can’t trust AI CEOs
articles.summary: Helen Toner, who studies AI safety and policy, says if we need to take AI warnings seriously, and we can’t rely on the tech industry to fix the problem.
articles.body: Today, I’m talking with Helen Toner, the executive director of the Center for Security and Emerging Technology at Georgetown University. This episode is part two of our series on AI in real life. Helen is a well-known figure in the AI safety and policy community, though she is perhaps best known for having served on the board of OpenAI, when she was one of four board members who voted to fire Sam Altman. That incident, now sometimes referred to as “the blip,” ended with Sam coming back as CEO, Helen resigning, and a new board of directors. OpenAI has since restructured entirely. But it’s worth remembering what Helen and the board were supposed to do: OpenAI’s nonprofit board existed specifically to make sure the company didn’t betray its mission to build safe AI by prioritizing profit and growth over safety. When the board actually tried to pull the lever, that accountability mechanism broke, and here we are. --- [Image: Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here. Not a subscriber? You can sign up here. --- Now, the question of AI safety is everywhere. This summer, AI models from OpenAI and Anthropic broke out of their testing environments and hacked real companies. The CEOs of these frontier labs have since called for a slowdown and asked Washington for help, but the White House’s answer was a voluntary accord — one that relies in part on the kind of board accountability that failed at OpenAI. Anthropic is also about to go public, which will put a whole new set of market pressures on OpenAI’s biggest competitor. Helen has seen up close what happens when safety commitments run headlong into commercial incentives. And as she put it to me, if our hopes for the future depend on any one person being trustworthy, we’re in big trouble. So we talked about what we might do instead: what the labs are actually trying to build, whether AI alignment is a problem that can be solved, and what a smarter approach to AI regulation might look like. That includes how to think about China, which is the issue that looms large in every policy conversation about AI right now — especially now after the Jensen Huang affair. Just for clarity, Helen and I talked before Nvidia opened its investigation and Jensen ultimately resigned, so you won’t hear us talk about that directly. Before we get going, do me a favor and subscribe to Decoder on YouTube, where we put out new episodes every Monday and Thursday. Okay: Helen Toner, the executive director of CSET, on the future of AI safety. Here we go. This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity. Helen Toner, you’re the executive director for the Center for Security and Emerging Technology at Georgetown University. Welcome to Decoder. Thanks so much. Great to be here. I have wanted to talk to you for 10 million years. I am so excited you’re here. You’ve been involved in a lot of AI safety and ethics ideas for a long time. You were obviously on the board of OpenAI during what everyone has come to call “the blip.” Now, you’re talking a lot about AI safety, about which I have 10 million questions. But let’s just start at the start. You run the Center for Security and Emerging Technology, people call it CSET. What is CSET? It’s awesome to be here. I’m really excited to talk to you as well. CSET is a team inside Georgetown, but we’re really not academics. We’re about 50 people and have been going since 2019. Basically in 2019, a group of us decided that there was a lot happening and a lot of emerging technologies that were becoming very relevant in the national security space, and the security space more broadly,. And some policymakers who had very important jobs did not have the time or the expertise to get across what was going on with those emerging technologies. Already at the top of our list in 2019 was AI. Basically our mission is to do analysis that is really rigorous, but also actionable, for policymakers and analysis that is both grounded in the technology and grounded in real national security expertise and understanding and issues. We produce long reports. We go do short briefings on those long reports to busy policymakers. We have a big data team that helps us do our research. We do all kinds of cool stuff. Can I just ask about the dynamics of that for one minute? You and I are talking the day after the midterm elections in the United States of America, and there was a big blue wave. There’s a lot of polling that says the number one issue is corruption. We’re going to throw the bums out. We’re going to start over and get rid of these corrupt guys. The AI industry, and the tech industry, has flooded a bunch of money into politics. And then somewhere next to that is, “Oh, there’s a bunch of well-meaning researchers who are going to show up and tell you how it actually works and what the real risks are.” It just occurs to me that maybe people don’t believe that’s effective anymore, that the money and the corruption and the AI CEO standing next to Trump have completely outweighed the well-meaning, sincere, “here are the actual problems” research that you do. What is that dynamic actually like? It’s a reasonable concern to have, and there are definitely some spaces where money just absolutely overwhelms everything. I’m Australian. I didn’t grow up in the US, and so the amount of money in US elections is pretty mind-blowing to me, but there are limits to what money can do. AI is a great example. In this election, there were just unbelievable amounts of money being thrown at candidates, at messages, at opposition research. There was all kinds of astroturfing on Twitter, and some very strange things trying to get anyone who talked about AI governance, regulation, safety, any of those words thrown out or not elected. It turns out to have really not worked very well. I think the reason that it didn’t work very well is one, this is an issue that voters increasingly care about. And two, also interestingly, it’s an issue that is pretty bipartisan at this point. What we see in our work is that there is a real thirst among policymakers for high-quality information. That’s members of Congress for sure, but they’re also in the executive branch, just a lot of people who have these very busy jobs and are seeing AI playing a larger and larger role in their work and their world. In DC, if you live and work here, you know that lobbyists in DC are not just people who go in and push their company’s position, though they do do that. They’re also educators. A big reason that congressional staff and others want to have lobbyists come talk to them is because they’ll really help them understand the weeds of a given piece of legislation — what does it mean for that industry and so on and so forth. What we find over and over again is we can go in and say, “Hey, we are independent. We’re nonpartisan. We do really rigorous work. We’re just here to help and we can go into the weeds with you as well.” There’s a ton of interest in that and appetite for that. It’s been really encouraging over the past seven to eight years. Are you doing that with the principals, the members of Congress, or are you doing that with the staff? Everyone and anyone. Again, we do a good amount of work with Congress on Capitol Hill, with some members of Congress, with lots of staff. We do hearings and briefings. Also, we do lots in the executive branch, with different agencies — the White House, Department of War, Department of State, Department of Commerce, all across the board at different levels, depending on the topic and what’s happening at any given moment. The reason I’m starting here is I want to have a pretty heady conversation with you, but I know what our audience thinks and it’s just that the government doesn’t get it. There’s no way the government will ever catch up to the tech industry. There’s no way they’ll ever write a regulation. They should just get out of the way. In this election cycle, I’ve seen a number of candidate forum videos where someone was like, “I’ve tried Claude once.” There’s some huge gap, real or perceived. I’m just trying to understand how you see that gap, how big you think that gap is, because as we get into AI safety and regulation, it’s that gap that has to close. There absolutely is a gap. It absolutely is a big gap. It also is possible to overestimate the gap from outside, or if you’re just looking across from California. I lived in the Bay Area for three years, so I definitely am very familiar with this perspective. I know a lot of people from the tech industry who come over and start talking to congressional staff or staffers in executive branch offices. Once they actually start having those conversations, they’re like, “Wow, these people are really smart. The staff do actually know what they’re talking about.” With principals, it is a different issue. Some of them are in the older generations, but they’re also getting smart. It takes time and it takes effort, and these people have so many demands on their time. The cynical thing to say is they’re just busy trying to get elected, but a lot of people in these roles also just have really big other topics that they have to be thinking about. They have to be thinking about wars and healthcare and cost of living and they’re looking at a lot of other stuff from day to day. I saw after ChatGPT, there was a wave in 2023 of, “Oh, maybe Congress is going to get activated on AI, maybe they’re going to actually do something.” It didn’t really turn into anything actually happening, but it did turn into a real moment where a lot of members of Congress and other policymakers started to get smart on AI. It takes some time to learn what a language model is. What even is AI? What is machine learning? They put in some of that work in 2023. I think this year we’re seeing another big wave of interest and people making the time and making the headspace to get smarter on it. I definitely don’t want to say there’s no gap or the government is super smart on AI across the board, but there are some champions who are really smart. I think the staff are generally smarter than people give them credit for. In my mind, it’s much more a question of, “Can the institutions, in the state of functionality that they’re in, get anything significant across the line?” more than, “Are these people just too behind the eight ball?” We’re going to see. There’s a whole bunch of new people. I imagine you have a new cast of characters to go and brief about the technology and what it’s capable of. We’ll see if they have revitalized the institutions. [Laughs] I’m sure it’ll be all fixed overnight. They’re very excited today, but we’ll see how it goes. The other thing that I want to ask you about is the technology itself, the nature of the technology itself, and how you are thinking about it, and the nature of the companies that are making the technology. The reason I’m asking that is I feel like there’s a pretty huge gap in the AI tools and systems most people experience and the way this industry thinks about it. My favorite example of this is we have straight-up asked Anthropic if it thinks Claude is alive and the answer was not no. The answer was a long discursion into the nature of the word “alive.” Well, it depends on what you mean by “alive” to start with. It does. And their answer was, “You need blood.” And I looked at that and I was like, “Who was talking about blood? It wasn’t us. Why are we talking about the requirement of flesh and blood to be alive?” And then some further conversation about the moral status of Claude is yet to be determined. There’s a huge divergence here between the AI overviews most people experience in Google search and “the moral status of Claude is uncertain.” Where are you? How are you situated in that debate? A big part of how I see our role at CSET as an organization, and then also my role as someone who is crossed between these worlds, is trying to translate and voyage to California and then bring back the artifacts and the recountings of my journey. I definitely think that there are a lot of people who have used the free tier of ChatGPT, or they’ve used voice-based models, which generally do worse, or they’ve just used Google AI overviews and they’ve laughed at how stupid Google AI overviews are. They haven’t used agents and they don’t know what frontier models can do. So there is just a basic piece around what the current generation of models can do. There’s a historical piece as well, which I find increasingly relevant as I’m now 10 years into working on AI and national security stuff. If you’re looking at this current moment in time, this snapshot, and saying, “Well, AI seems kind of cool, but it can’t do X,” you have to situate that in the long history of people being like, “Well, AI seems kind of cool, but it can’t do X,” for many, many values of X that have since become totally overcome by events. You can go back and say, “Okay, well, here’s how we were talking about creativity, for example, five or 10 years ago.” Or we were talking about reasoning as this insurmountable thing before you had these new models come out. A huge thing that I am spending time on these days is not just the past and present of AI, but how companies are thinking about what they’re doing, especially the two leading companies, OpenAI and Anthropic, and this is true at Google, Meta, SpaceX to some extent as well. This idea in the Bay Area that it’s just in the water, very normalized of, “Well, first we’re going to figure out how to do recursive self-improvement (RSI) and then we’re going to do that until we have superintelligence that is AI that vastly outstrips humans.” That’s taken for granted in a lot of circles at this point. I think there’s still a ton of alpha in just taking the fact that that is what they’re trying to do and just explaining what that means. It takes a little while to lay out. “What is RSI? Why would you want to do that? What is superintelligence? What does that mean? Is that realistic?” All of that. But it is something I find myself spending a lot of time on these days, and something that there is increasing willingness to take seriously and to listen to in DC as well. Lay that out for me. I think probably a lot of people listening to this show understand what you’re talking about, but we have a big audience. What do you mean by, “We’re going to do RSI and that will lead to superintelligence?” The starting point here is these companies, especially OpenAI and Anthropic, were not set up to be consumer internet companies. A lot of people encountered this whole space after ChatGPT was launched. So the natural slot in their brain that they put a company like OpenAI or Anthropic into is a consumer tech company, where they have an app and I play with their app. I cannot overstate how far that is from the vision of both companies when they started, and also the vision deep in the hearts of some of the top people at both of those companies. The vision deep in their hearts is we’re going to build machines that are as smart as or smarter than people. That is going to be amazing and it’s going to be a huge scientific achievement and it’s going to revolutionize the world and we’re going to be at the forefront of that and we’re going to do everything we possibly can to drive towards that. That’s not a totally brand-new thing. We don’t have to do the whole history of AI, but it started as a field in roughly the 1950s with this idea of whether you can recreate human intelligence inside a machine. That’s kind of the starting point. If we’re talking about people like Sam Altman and Dario Amodei, but also the core people inside, the researchers inside their labs, so your Alec Radfords or your John Schulmans or people like that, that is the vision that got them into this space that is motivating everything that they do. That’s been true since the beginning, since OpenAI was founded in 2015 and Anthropic in 2021. These days, the point that they’re getting to is this idea of RSI, recursive self-improvement, which again, is a very old idea. In the 1960s, this guy called I. J. Good, who worked with Alan Turing, talks about the possibility that you could build an ultra-intelligent machine, meaning a machine that is more intelligent than any human, and then that could build an even more intelligent machine and that could build an even more intelligent machine, which would kick off what he calls an intelligence explosion, meaning that the level of intelligence of the systems is exploding. For decades and decades and decades, this was this theoretical idea of, “Well, if the AI gets smart enough, maybe it can take over building the next generation of AI or directly improving itself.” I think 2025 and 2026, we’ve started to see AI companies saying, “Okay, yeah, this theoretical idea… we’re actually starting to be able to do a minimal version of it in practice.” It’s not handing over all the AI development to the AI, and it’s certainly not saying to GPT-6, like, “Okay, GPT-6, improve yourself.” That’s not what they’re doing. But they are progressively using AI for more and more parts of their overall R&D pipeline, and they are increasingly saying that they’re seeing acceleration from that. They’re seeing their own R&D getting faster and faster. A lot of people elsewhere doubt this, but a lot of people inside the companies really think it. When Demis Hassabis says “we’re in the foothills of the singularity,” this is the kind of thing he means: We might be seeing that initial part of the exponential curve where the AI systems are building the next generation of smarter and smarter systems such that the hockey stick then goes up. At this point, it’s been a part of the culture and a part of the goals for so long that I think people in these companies can lose sight of how totally insane that sounds to many, many people. So I feel like there’s a lot of value in just trying to lay out, “Here’s what they are trying to do. They might not be able to do it, but they might be,” and presenting that to a range of different people. How would you manage that? Demis Hassabis saying “foothills of the singularity” is an all-time quote. I’m not 100 percent sure the people at Google knew he was going to say that on stage to end the conference. Greg Brockman, president of OpenAI, announced a new version of the model a few months ago, and he was like, “Here it is. It’s Astra. It’s AGI now. Have a good time.” And he ended the call. Are you there? Are we at AGI? Is this already here and we just haven’t noticed? I actually wrote something about this. I do not want to say we have AGI. I do want to say we’ve reached the point where I think using AGI as a milestone is just totally unhelpful. The way I put it is the concept of AGI is kind of a fuzzy cloud, which you could think of as different parts of the cloud or different things people mean by AGI. There are people who’ve complained about the term AGI for a long time. Ten years ago it was pretty helpful to be able to say, “Look, the AI systems we have today in 2016, they can all only do one thing and they can recognize speech or they can play Go or whatever, but we’re trying to build this bigger thing that we’re going to call AGI, which is human-level and it’s going to be so general purpose. It’s going to be amazing.” That was a useful term then because this fuzzy cloud of different things AGI might mean was so far away, so you could just point at the fuzzy cloud. But at this point, we’re inside that cloud, meaning we’ve passed some definitions of AGI. A very basic one, for instance, would be even when ChatGPT came out as an artificial general intelligence. ChatGPT was very clearly not a specialist model that was only good at one thing, like recognizing credit card fraud or translation or whatever. It could do many, many, many things. So we’ve reached some definitions of AGI. We’re far from other definitions. Some people will say AGI is when it awakens and is sentient and can do every single thing that any human ever can do. I think we’re pretty far from that. At this point you can have arguments, and people do have arguments, of “well, Astra is AGI,” or “was [OpenAI’s] o3 with tools AGI” or “was ChatGPT AGI,” whatever. If that’s the argument we’re having, we just need to set aside that term and come up with different, more-specific things we mean by that.” The president wants to call it “Super Intelligence.” I don’t know if you’ve heard. [Laughs] I have heard. The thing I find saddest about that is just that it was an existing term that is becoming increasingly relevant. I have a lot of feelings about words and terminology. Are you AGI-pilled? Do you think we’re going to get there in the current run of technology? I think it is obviously possible enough that we need to think seriously about it, which is my stance on a lot of this weird stuff. I’m not like, “This is definitely happening, it’s definitely happening in two years.” But I’m like, “Look, I think this is very solidly plausible and very solidly in the realm of real things that could happen that we should prepare for.” I work in the national security space. There’s things like, “Will China launch a full-scale amphibious invasion of Taiwan?” where most analysts in the space will say “probably not,” and “probably they would lose.” Also, “We would see signs of them preparing and whatever, but we should take that seriously.” We should not just laugh anyone out of the room and call that science fiction. We should be ready for a range of different contingencies and scenarios. Do you think Claude is conscious? I have no idea. That’s an answer. I mean, that is legitimately an answer. It is scientifically such an unsolved problem. What do we mean by consciousness? And is that a thing or is it actually 10 different things that we’re lumping together or what? I have no idea. What do you think? No. I seem to be the person in this ecosystem who gets asked questions like that and I’m like, “No.” Because the thing that I struggle with is, there are lots of other things where we’re already confused about whether they’re conscious. So with animals, are any animals conscious? And if so, which ones? Insects? This is why I understand why Anthropic was like, “Does it have blood?” And then you can just draw the line. I’m like, “I think I’m there and I understand why the mirror test of talking to a computer that can talk to you leads one to believe that these things are conscious.” My point of view is that the frontier models to me sometimes feel brittle in the way that computers feel brittle, and the sign of consciousness I’m looking for is to overcome that brittleness. That’s interesting. I definitely lean towards no, it’s not conscious. I think something that is really, really tough in this space is that it’s really bad if you get it wrong in either direction. If the computers aren’t conscious and we treat them as though they are, we’re going to make all kinds of terrible decisions. But if the computers are conscious, meaning in some sense they should be worthy of moral consideration and it matters how well we treat them and so on, and we treat them as though they aren’t, then that’s also a really huge, terrible disaster. So I don’t know. I feel pretty nervous about the whole topic and I have no idea how to think about it. The reason I’m asking these questions is I started with what the nature of the regulator is. Who are the people that might be able to put some rules in place? And then what is the nature of the thing that we are attempting to regulate? And if your answer is “Claude is alive,” you’re going to come to vastly different conclusions than, “We have built some ultra-powerful computers that can take actions without oversight and that might not be connected to our goals.” I think that’s right. Though I also think people make a different mistake.I just heard a TV anchor do this the other night. They’ll conflate different things. So they’ll say, “Do you think that AI systems are at risk of running amuck and causing damage to critical infrastructure because they’re sentient?” And I’m like, “Wait, wait, wait. Those are two very different things.” So I agree with you. One of the most fascinating things about the project of building AI is that we’re learning as we go. All these things that we thought were connected to each other aren’t necessarily connected to each other. An old version of this is, people said before we had chess engines: “Well, if a computer could learn to play chess, it would have learned something deep about strategy.” No, it turns out definitely not. You can just put in a bunch of chess moves and it learns nothing generalizable about strategy. It goes in the reverse direction as well, like, “Well, it’s just a computer, it’s just math, and so it’s not going to be able to adapt on the fly,” or something. We then see that no, once you do have a level of long-horizon autonomy and the models have been trained on a wide range of different really hard problems where the environment is changing around them, they can learn to adapt and come up with different plans on the fly and troubleshoot and so on. So I don’t know. I try to have a level of humility about how confident we can be that one thing goes with another thing, if that makes sense. Yeah, candidly, I have been wrong about the limits of LLMs every single year, but there’s that brittleness that I’m talking about. OpenAI solved Navier-Stokes. Does the model know this? Will it know that there’s new problems to solve? I don’t think so. The next model will know it. The model that’s pretrained. Right. But you have to make a new one. Yeah. That’s a very weird dynamic, and that is probably where you enforce the regulation. There’s “what we are going to let you do with the models you have today” and “what will you teach the models of the future to do?” And if you think that they’re conscious, you end up in a moral quandary, not a legislative quandary. Definitely. Yeah, totally. This is what I mean. Actually, it’s the heart of this question for me. I’ve been just slowly building up to it. I’m not 100 percent sure alignment as we have it today is actually how you solve the safety problem. It doesn’t seem to be working. We seem to be attacking Hugging Face however we want. That feels like a technology problem. That gap is there. And when you say alignment, what do you mean by that? Just sort of the very basic common-sense version of “we’re going to tell the model to not be evil” or Anthropic is going to write a Claude constitution that’s like, “You are a good person.” However we think of alignment in that very dumb system prompt way. Maybe there’s another better way to think about it, but that’s how I have always thought about it. That makes sense. The reason I ask is I feel like alignment as a concept is... Like I said, I hate all the words. I sometimes say we should just ban all the words, no words allowed. It covers too much. People in AI will often talk about solving this or solving that. So it’ll be solving alignment, or DeepMind’s original mission was to solve intelligence, then use that to solve everything else. People talk about solving stuff. I don’t know that alignment is a thing that can be solved. Some people use “alignment” to mean “the company can put on guardrails and the guardrails work,” meaning the model doesn’t do what you want because the company tried to ban it, meaning biological weapons or cyberattacks or whatever. Some people use “alignment” to mean “the company does exactly what the user wants,” which is the reverse. And some people use “alignment” to mean what you said — that the model is morally good in some kind of broad way or can direct the future in a way that will lead to human flourishing or something. Those are just wildly different things to try and build. I think the most coherent one is trying to get the AI to do what the user wanted it to do. It seems like that is, as far as I can tell, not on track to be solved, which is not great, to put it mildly. To me, this is the core problem. We’re going to talk about a bunch of safety risks. You mentioned bioweapons. We probably should not give a bunch of consumers paying $20 a month the ability to generate novel bioweapons. It feels like that is a shared policy goal, maybe the only bipartisan policy goal in America. And then I’m like, “How? By what means will we implement this policy? Are you just going to sternly tell Claude to not do it? Do you have to build an AI control system on top of Claude to monitor the inputs and outputs? Do the police have to be at my house? Do I need a Flock camera above my keyboard?” How, specifically, would you do it? With this one, and with cyber capabilities as well, there’s a perspective in some parts of the AI safety community that some capabilities are just too dangerous — capital T, capital D, Too Dangerous. So you have to do something, because if they proliferate, everything will be terrible forever because there’ll be so many attacks and so much damage. I think that just underestimates the level of dynamism and the finding of equilibriums and responses and ways that society can adapt. In the bioweapons case, for example, there are already hundreds of thousands of people in the US who know how to make bioweapons because they’ve been through biology training, and we don’t have huge amounts of bioweapons attacks. Some part of that is that that knowledge is relatively scarce, but there’s also a lot around things like access to materials, the ability to do mail-order DNA synthesis; the kind of policy you could implement is restricting mail-order DNA synthesis. If we don’t get there first, then we’ll never get the nonproliferation treaty that we need to keep us all safe for mutually assured destruction. That’s one framework. Way on the other end, I spent five years of my life listening to telecom executives tell me that if we didn’t build 5G networks first, China would get them, and then something. No one could ever tell me what the “something” was. Where on that spectrum between 5G and nuclear weapons is the US-China AI race? I think we need another dimension because in that example, your dimension is significance. But I think the controllability is a huge question as well. So it’s like, what are the examples that people use? Is it a nuclear weapon or is it dragons from House of the Dragon? Casey Newton had a great Platformer post where he explained he was watching House of the Dragon and thought, “This is what the AI companies are doing. They’re trying to build these things that they think will help them, but actually it’s just going to rain down destruction.” [Laughs] Casey told me he was buying an iPhone Duo so he could watch more TV. He’s a dear friend, but okay. But I think that’s really important because if we think this is a technology we can control, then obviously we want to have the best technology. Obviously, we want to go foot to the floor, get there as fast as we can, and the same is true for China. The question is, if we are not sure if we can control it, then what do we do? Maybe we want to be more cautious and then maybe we want to try and figure out a way to not have China just be overtaking us. But if we’re correct we should be worried about— So that’s nuclear weapons. Well, no, but if it’s dragons, if we’re correct that we need to be worried about whether we can control this, then that’s also something that should be interesting to China. I remember this Casey post, but let me just try to pull this apart so I understand it. The difference between dragons and nuclear weapons is the dragons have some agency, right? They can go away and do bad things on their own. Yes. The dragons might just decide to burn down your whole city. Obviously these are machines — they’re just math, they’re not magical. So instead of dragons, you could think of it as nuclear weapons with faulty control settings, where you build nuclear weapons, but it’s impossible to be sure that it’s not just going to go off and fly to a city and fly to one of your own cities and wipe you out. That’s a very different technology than real nuclear weapons that exist. It is true. No one ever said that about 5G. I’ll be clear about that. The reason I’m asking about this is because those problems do align nation-states, right? We do have nuclear nonproliferation agreements. As you mentioned, there are all kinds of incentives for nation-states to not do cyberattacks willy-nilly because those have real-world consequences. Is there any evidence that these governments have started to align on these problems? Or is it still the pure “But China!” race dynamic? I actually think there is starting to be some early evidence. One way I think about what happened this year in AI from a policy perspective, less than a product or economic perspective, is we saw these two big demonstrations of the two major concerns people have. So the two major concerns are misuse and misalignment, meaning misuse is bad people using AI for bad things and misalignment is AI going rogue or doing things we didn’t want. So this year we had Mythos and we had the Hugging Face attack. Both of those are just really vivid, crisp real-world demonstrations of what these misuse and misalignment concerns could look like. The US and Chinese governments are starting from very different places on AI regulation. They’re both starting from where they started, and what they did with, internet regulation. So the US is starting from a “hands off, laissez-faire, absolutely nothing, do whatever you want” approach. China is starting from a massively locked-down internet with tons of censorship and the Great Firewall. So those are two very different starting points. I’m not a China expert, but I operate a lot in China circles and I’ve lived in China and so on. But it seems like just over the past even one to three months, starting from those two very different points, they are seeing more in common around threats from major cyberattacks and also threats of loss of control. I’m a language nerd and it’s really interesting tracking the different language China uses about AI. So they’re now talking about loss of control as a thing, but they probably usually don’t mean the same thing that Westerners mean where “loss of control” is like “AI takeover.” They probably mean something more prosaic, but then sometimes they talk about “extreme loss of control,” which maybe is the thing we mean. I do think that there are starting to be some signs of convergence. I think it’ll be a long road. The state of the US-China relationship is such that there’s going to be very, very, very little trust on either side. So I am not optimistic that they’ll just get to sit down in a room and hash out a deal and everything will be great. But I think there is enough space. Basically, if there’s enough shared threat perception, then it might be possible at some point in the future to do something about that. Helen, you’ve given me so much time. As you can tell, I’m just delighted with this conversation. It’s been very fun. We are on the cusp of a new Congress. There are a bunch of new governors. The data center referendums passed overwhelmingly in this country. There’s a new set of regulators in town, right? They’re going to do some stuff. What are some signs people should look for to indicate we’re going to be on the right path and what are some signs that we’re just chasing our tail? Set AI aside, forget about AI. Congress in general is very bad at passing things right now. This is not a this administration thing, this is not an AI thing. So one sign is like, can Congress pass anything? That will be a good sign. It’s also really interesting to look at what state legislatures have been doing in AI. There’s been a lot of concern about the possibility of a state patchwork on AI, with different states passing conflicting things. With the issues that we’ve been talking about today, which I think of as frontier AI risks or the risks from the most advanced systems, there’s actually been a pretty coordinated push in different states. California passed this one bill and then New York passed almost the same bill with just a little more added to it. And then Illinois passed almost the same bill with a little more added to it. I think there’s going to be a lot of momentum over the next year or two to keep building on that at the state level. So that is something that I’ll be watching. Even just specifically California is already looking at how they can strengthen things. So that is something I’ll be looking for. I think honestly, with such a Democratic Congress, I am also concerned that they will overstep here, that they will try and do something that is too sweeping. You had this huge mess in Colorado where they passed this giant AI bill that then was a terrible idea. And so then they had all these committees and follow-up and it was awful. A lot of what we need right now is focused on these frontier systems and the possibility that we have really, really advanced systems in a short amount of time and having much more transparency around that and much clearer standards for how they manage risk. I would not be that excited about an attempt to do a really comprehensive AI regulatory push that covers AI all across the economy and all different kinds of AI systems that are less advanced. There are negative signals that are like “nothing’s going to happen,” and there are negative signals like, “oh, maybe too much is going to happen,” but it’ll be interesting to see where they get to. I suspect we’re going to want to have you back as this Congress starts to get to work and we see some of these ideas. I would love to. I’m eager for your take on it. Thank you so much for being on Decoder. Thanks so much. This was really fun. Questions or comments? Hit us up at decoder@theverge.com. We really do read every email!
