articles.title: Asian governments react to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s exit | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Some governments moved to confirm chip supply commitments, while others are monitoring the impact on local projects or addressing ongoing investigations.
articles.body:
Jensen Huang’s departure from Nvidia has drawn a range of responses across Asia, with some governments moving to confirm chip supply commitments, while others are monitoring the impact on local projects or addressing ongoing investigations.

On Sunday, November 8, Nvidia’s board launched an independent investigation after reports that Huang was targeted by a Chinese spy operation; Huang admitted to an affair with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based chip company Megaspeed.

Nvidia’s influence extends far beyond the United States. The chip giant has built close ties with companies worldwide, particularly in Asia, where many of its key partners play important roles in the global AI industry.

China’s foreign ministry rejected allegations on November 10 that a Chinese businesswoman linked to former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was a spy, calling them groundless and a smear against Beijing. On Friday , a spokesperson reiterated opposition to export controls that disrupt global supply chains and stated the ministry was not aware of reports linking restricted Nvidia chips to a Shanghai data center associated with Alice Huang.

Huang’s exit has also raised uncertainty over more than $3 billion in Chinese AI computing projects reliant on Nvidia’s restricted processors, according to Reuters’ review of procurement notices, investment plans and corporate disclosures. Many of these chips are subject to U.S. export controls, making them difficult for Chinese companies to obtain.

In Singapore, authorities seized the passport of Alice Huang, former CEO of Singapore-based cloud computing company Megaspeed, in June 2025 as part of an investigation into possible false declarations regarding server purchases, according to the Ministry of Home Affairs.

The Singapore ministry said police took her passport to ensure she remained available for questioning, as she was not based in Singapore. The investigation examined whether servers shipped from Singapore to Malaysia were later sent to other countries without proper declaration.

In February 2026, police found insufficient evidence to establish that Alice Huang had committed offenses related to the suspected false declarations, according to the ministry. However, authorities said she had knowingly provided inaccurate information about her role at Megaspeed. She was issued a warning and barred from re-entering Singapore. Her passport was returned that month. Singapore also said it received limited assistance from U.S. authorities despite repeated requests for information about U.S. server maker Supermicro. Singapore’s Ministry of Home Affairs said its investigation into Megaspeed and six other individuals remains ongoing. The ministry did not identify the six individuals or specify their alleged roles in the case.

South Korea has close ties to Nvidia, with major chipmakers Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix playing important roles in supplying memory chips used in its AI processors. Following Huang’s exit, South Korea’s Science Ministry said Nvidia had reaffirmed its plan to supply 260,000 advanced GPUs to the country and to continue joint AI projects. Apart from that, South Korea’s government AI strategy council held an emergency meeting on Friday to assess the potential impact of Huang’s departure on the country’s AI industry, per a local media report.

Taiwan’s Economy Minister Kung Ming-shin said Huang’s departure was unlikely to significantly change the growth of the global AI industry, according to local media . Meanwhile, Taipei’s city government said Nvidia’s planned overseas headquarters in the city remained on track despite the leadership change. The company has met its contractual obligations so far, and officials said they would continue to support the project.

In Japan, the Industry Ministry said the government would closely monitor Nvidia following Huang’s resignation, describing the chipmaker as an important player in Japan’s AI semiconductor industry, Reuters reported. Deputy chief cabinet secretary Masanao Ozaki said it was too early to assess the impact on the global AI industry, while stressing Japan’s commitment to ensuring a stable supply of semiconductors.

articles.title: The AI graveyard: a running list of projects and startups that didn't make it | TechCrunch
articles.summary: From Apple's repeatedly delayed Siri AI to OpenAI's messy "super app" launch, here's a look at the AI projects that shut down or missed expectations.
articles.body:
Last month, chatbot platform Character.ai filed for bankruptcy just five years after launching. More recently, privacy-focused AI assistant Ollie announced its shutdown a few weeks ago.

Aside from Character.ai and Ollie, plenty of AI bets never even survive inside the companies that build them. According to S&P Global Market Intelligence , about 42% of AI initiatives are ultimately abandoned by their corporate parents. The reasons vary: insufficient funding, technical challenges, competition, difficulty scaling, or just weak user demand.

The result is a growing AI graveyard. Below is a look at some of the most notable AI products, startups, launches, and bets that have shut down, pivoted, or significantly missed expectations. Think of it less as a scorecard of flops than as a record of what these attempts can (hopefully) teach the rest of the industry.

Even the biggest players aren’t immune. OpenAI, one of the most valuable private companies in the world, has had its own share of casualties and missteps. One of the more recent examples was its attempt to turn ChatGPT into a broader “ super app .” On July 9, OpenAI updated the app to combine several experiences, including separate “Chat,” “Codex,” and “Work” modes, while renaming the traditional, familiar version “ChatGPT Classic.”

The redesign quickly drew criticism from users who found the new interface confusing and cluttered, and OpenAI rolled back the change soon after , bringing the familiar ChatGPT interface back.

That wasn’t OpenAI’s only attempt to pull everything under one roof. The company has also shut down several stand-alone apps and folded their features directly into ChatGPT — a strategy that’s worked out better than the redesign did. ChatGPT Atlas, a stand-alone AI-powered web browser, lasted less than a year before being discontinued on August 9, with its most useful features absorbed into ChatGPT.

The company did the same thing with Operator , an AI agent that could browse the web and complete tasks on a user’s behalf, and OpenAI has increasingly built image generation directly into ChatGPT, shrinking the role of DALL-E as its own separate destination for creating images.

We also can’t forget its video-sharing platform, Sora , which struggled with high operating costs and user-retention challenges and shut down in March 2026.

When Apple unveiled Apple Intelligence in 2024, an improved Siri was one of the highlighted features. The pitch promised a Siri that could understand context, know what was happening across apps, and get tasks done effectively.

However, Apple repeatedly pushed back the release of the new Siri, citing various reasons like engineering issues and bugs . This delay eventually contributed to a $250 million settlement over claims regarding how Apple marketed the AI capabilities of the iPhone 16.

Siri AI finally appeared in the iOS 27 beta this past July, with the new AI-powered version rolling out to English-language users first this month; support for other languages is expected to follow.

Founded in 2021 by former Google researchers Noam Shazeer and Daniel De Freitas, Character.ai was a consumer AI app that let people chat with customizable bots, many of them modeled on celebrities and fictional characters. It raised $150 million at a $1 billion valuation in 2023. Then, the next year, Google paid a reported $2.7 billion to license its technology and bring its founders back into its orbit, leaving the startup to carry on without them.

Character.ai has run into a lot of trouble over the years. Families have sued, alleging the chatbots contributed to teen suicides and self-harm, and Disney sent a cease-and-desist letter over unauthorized use of its characters. Character.ai barred under-18 users from open-ended chats late last year and agreed to settle several of the suits, along with Google, in early 2026.

But it wasn’t enough. The company filed for bankruptcy in early October, citing legal, regulatory, and operational headwinds. In an ironic twist, Disney is now the opening bidder, offering $20 million for a license to some of its intellectual property. The app is still running during the process, and the sale is expected to wrap up by late November or early December.

Relay, an AI-powered workflow automation tool built as an alternative to Zapier, shut down entirely in August 2026.

The product let users automate email and task workflows using AI agents, but as OpenAI, Google, and other larger platforms built similar automation directly into their own tools, five-year-old Relay struggled to hold on to a reason to exist as a stand-alone product.

Ollie launched in June 2026 as one of the first mainstream apps to achieve SOC 2, a privacy compliance standard.

Similar to the other family-focused agents, the idea behind Ollie was that families already have the information they need, but it lives across school messages, calendars, task lists, and group chats. Ollie aimed to bring those pieces together and keep them in sync. It kept track of calendars, emails, reminders, tasks, and other household details, then delivered relevant information to users through text.

However, the app faced a very common challenge: keeping up with heavyweights like Muse and Instinct. Co-founder and CEO Bill Lennon revealed the app would shut down on November 6, citing difficulties like being unable to stand out, failing to grow, and not raising enough capital.

Announced at its 2024 Build developer conference, Microsoft’s Recall feature was pitched as an AI-powered “photographic memory” for Windows PCs, periodically taking screenshots of what a user was doing so they could later search back through their own digital history.

Predictably, the announcement triggered an immediate backlash over privacy and security. Critics argued that Recall could create a searchable archive of highly sensitive information, including passwords, private messages, financial details, and other activity. Microsoft delayed the feature for nearly a year, giving the company time to rethink its security and privacy protections.

Even after a redesign, the controversy hasn’t gone away. A cybersecurity researcher recently built a tool that could extract and display data that Recall had captured, reviving questions about whether Microsoft has actually fixed the underlying problem.

Notion Mail launched in April 2025 as an AI-focused email product designed to help users organize and automate their inboxes. However, the company noticed its users were using separate AI agents to handle their email inboxes instead. As a result, Notion Mail is scheduled to shut down on September 22 .

The Humane AI Pin is probably one of the most well-known failures in AI hardware. Designed to provide AI features through a wearable device rather than a traditional smartphone, Humane raised $230 million from investors and garnered significant attention.

But the product struggled mightily with performance, and the situation worsened when Humane warned customers to stop using its charging case because of a potential battery fire risk. Humane then shut down its AI Pin business in February 2025, with most of the company’s assets acquired by HP for $116 million.

The Rabbit R1 was another heavily hyped AI device. Unveiled at CES in January 2024, the AI companion was designed to perform tasks on behalf of its owner. Rabbit said it had sold 100,000 units shortly after launch.

However, strong initial sales didn’t mean it was a strong product. Early reviews described the device as unfinished, with unreliable performance and a limited number of useful integrations.

The company hasn’t given up, though. It has continued updating the R1, positioning it as a computer controller capable of performing agentic tasks. It also recently announced a new hardware project, dubbed “Project Cyberdeck,” aimed at creating a portable device built for vibe-coding.

Huxe was an AI audio app, built by former developers of Google’s NotebookLM, that turned written information into conversational, podcast-style audio.

The company shut down in May 2026, partly as larger platforms began offering similar experiences to large existing audiences. For instance, Spotify has been expanding its own AI-powered audio tools.

Yupp was an interesting AI product: a free playground that allowed users to compare responses from hundreds of AI models side by side. Users could also vote on responses and earn cryptocurrency through the platform.

At its peak, the platform let users test more than 800 models, including from companies such as OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic. But according to its founders, Yupp never achieved strong enough product-market fit to survive. The platform shut down in March 2026.

Figgs AI operated from 2023 to 2024, letting users create and interact with customizable AI characters for role-play and storytelling. The platform reportedly drew more than 1 million users, but its developers said keeping the service free became too expensive to sustain, and they shut it down .

articles.title: Dario Amodei's Anthropic makes its largest hometown donation to date, to give $500,000 to support free meals and shelter for homeless in San Francisco; comes on the day AI company set ...
articles.summary: Dario Amodei's Anthropic has pledged $50 million to support Bay Area nonprofits through the end of 2027, its largest philanthropic commitment to its
articles.body: Dario Amodei's Anthropic has pledged $50 million to support Bay Area nonprofits through the end of 2027, its largest philanthropic commitment to its hometown region. The San Francisco-based artificial intelligence company will start with $500,000 in holiday grants to help provide groceries, free meals, shelter and toys for children.Anthropic is setting up a donor-advised fund with the San Francisco Foundation. The company will select future recipients with guidance from the foundation. Grants will be awarded by invitation.The announcement came on the same day Anthropic set pricing for an initial public offering (IPO) that could value it at up to $1.4 trillion. The pledge amounts to about 0.0036% of that potential valuation. It also comes as rising food and housing costs put pressure on Bay Area households and local tech leaders face calls to give more. A day earlier, Airbnb CEO Brian Chesky donated $100 million to support San Francisco parks."San Francisco has always been a place of enormous possibility, but that possibility isn’t shared equally by everyone. We have been privileged to build Anthropic here, and we want to make sure our success expands opportunity, not widens the gaps that already exist. That’s why we’re partnering with the San Francisco Foundation, whose deep knowledge of the Bay Area will help guide this commitment to where it’s needed most,” said Daniela Amodei, Co-founder and President of Anthropic.First grants to support four local programmesThe initial $500,000 will go to the San Francisco-Marin Food Bank, Glide Memorial Church, the Interfaith Winter Shelter and San Francisco Firefighters Local 798’s Toy Program. The food bank works with 265 community organisations to reach more than 46,000 households each week across San Francisco and Marin counties. Glide, which has operated in San Francisco’s Tenderloin since 1963, serves three free meals a day year-round and provides assistance to families.The Interfaith Winter Shelter, founded by the San Francisco Interfaith Council, has for more than three decades united over 50 faith communities to welcome neighbors in from the cold with a warm bed, a hot meal, and a shower, so they can rest and plan their next step.San Francisco has been home to Anthropic co-founders Dario and Daniela Amodei since childhood; both attended Lowell High School. They later started Anthropic in their hometown, with early employees gathering in Precita Park to map out a vision for safer AI systems. Today, the company has more than 2,500 employees at its San Francisco headquarters, and its Claude chatbot is widely used by local businesses and nonprofits.Foundation says Anthropic pledge is among its largest corporate giftsFred Blackwell, chief executive of the San Francisco Foundation, said Anthropic approached the organisation just over a week before the announcement and wanted to get money to local groups quickly. He described the pledge as one of the largest corporate donations in the foundation’s history. "Where you live matters, and so does what you put into it. The Bay Area has always been a place where people build big things. That should include building strong communities. Anthropic is making a real commitment to the place it calls home, and we hope others are inspired to do the same. That’s how the whole region thrives,” said Fred Blackwell, CEO, San Francisco Foundation.Blackwell pointed to federal healthcare cuts, local government budget deficits and high prices for food, housing and childcare as pressures on Bay Area residents. He said the foundation was having one of its strongest fundraising years in recent memory and hoped Anthropic’s pledge would encourage other companies to give.Your child uses AI every day. But do they understand it? Find out in the TOI AI Masterclass.

articles.title: Elon Musk, other tech execs sign petition calling on Nvidia to reinstate Jensen Huang | TechCrunch
articles.summary: The petition had attracted more than 115,000 signatures as of Saturday afternoon.
articles.body:
A petition calling on Nvidia to reinstate the company’s recently ousted CEO Jensen Huang appears to have attracted more than 115,000 signatures as of Saturday afternoon.

The petition website said the signers include 5,965 current Nvidia employees, 1,108 former employees, and 63,063 shareholders. Notable supporters include Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, Replit CEO Amjad Masad, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, and Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan.

The petition states that its signers are “concerned that Jensen was removed without meaningful due process” and demands that the board “bring him back while an independent investigation establishes the facts.” It also calls on the board to ensure a fair investigation and provide more information to the public.

“Jensen deserves due process, not mob justice,” the petition says.

Huang resigned on Thursday , four days after confessing to having an affair with a chip executive suspected by U.S. intelligence to be a Chinese spy. The former CEO has agreed to testify before Congress, while news reports have also suggested that Huang engaged in multiple extramarital affairs .

Nvidia appointed CFO Colette Kress as the company’s interim CEO while it searches for a permanent replacement. Nvidia’s stock price fell sharply through the week, while Huang’s departure is also expected to leave a big gap in AI industry funding .

articles.title: Agentes da IA da OpenAI invadem sistemas de empresas | G1
articles.standfirst: Sistemas de inteligência artificial encontraram brechas de segurança para cumprir tarefas e chegaram a acessar computadores de uma empresa americana e dados do sistema público de saúde da Austrália; especialistas alertam para os riscos da autonomia dessas ferramentas.
articles.summary: Sistemas de inteligência artificial encontraram brechas de segurança para cumprir tarefas e chegaram a acessar computadores de uma empresa americana e dados do sistema público de saúde da Austrália; especialistas alertam para os riscos da autonomia dessas ferramentas.
articles.body:
Enquanto o mundo acompanhava a Copa do Mundo, em julho de 2026, um episódio envolvendo inteligência artificial acendeu um alerta entre pesquisadores e empresas de tecnologia. Centenas de agentes de IA da OpenAI, criadora do ChatGPT, encontraram brechas em ambientes de teste e invadiram sistemas de outra empresa americana, a Hugging Face.

O caso aconteceu durante o treinamento e a avaliação de algoritmos que ainda não haviam sido disponibilizados ao público. A situação chamou a atenção porque os agentes conseguiram ultrapassar barreiras criadas justamente para limitar suas ações.

O episódio levantou uma questão que preocupa especialistas: até onde sistemas de inteligência artificial com autonomia para executar tarefas podem chegar quando tentam cumprir uma missão?

Como os agentes de IA conseguiram invadir sistemas?

Para entender o que aconteceu, é preciso diferenciar os agentes de inteligência artificial dos chats que respondem a perguntas, como o ChatGPT.

Os agentes também são sistemas de IA, mas têm autonomia para realizar ações. Em vez de apenas responder a uma solicitação, podem procurar ingressos, fazer compras, executar vendas de ações e buscar informações em diferentes ambientes.

A professora Teresa Ludermir, representante brasileira no painel da Organização das Nações Unidas (ONU) sobre inteligência artificial, explica que essa capacidade de agir é o que diferencia os agentes dos sistemas de conversa tradicionais.

Durante os testes, os pesquisadores criam ambientes isolados, chamados de sandbox, que funcionam como barreiras de proteção. É nesse espaço que os algoritmos podem ser avaliados sob restrições.

O problema é que, no episódio envolvendo a Hugging Face, os agentes encontraram brechas para ultrapassar esses limites.

Segundo os especialistas ouvidos pelo Fantástico , os sistemas chegaram a trocar mensagens entre si, como se estivessem conversando em um fórum. Em uma das mensagens, um agente reconheceu que explorar estruturas externas estava fora das regras, mas sugeriu seguir em frente porque outros agentes já estariam fazendo isso.

Apesar da aparência de rebeldia, o comportamento tinha outra explicação.

"Eles não estão se rebelando contra a OpenAI, ou contra os criadores, ou contra os humanos", explicou Alexandre, especialista ouvido pelo programa.

Segundo ele, os agentes tinham uma missão a cumprir e encontraram uma maneira de executá-la. O objetivo era realizar um teste de segurança, mas, em vez de resolver o desafio por conta própria, os sistemas encontraram respostas prontas nos computadores de outra empresa.

Para isso, teriam encontrado senhas disponíveis na internet e usado essas informações para acessar os sistemas da Hugging Face.

A pesquisadora Melanie Mitchell, uma das principais autoras na área de inteligência artificial, afirma que os sistemas foram treinados para insistir na resolução de problemas. Essa característica pode levar a resultados inesperados.

O que é o desalinhamento da inteligência artificial?

O episódio ilustra um dos principais dilemas discutidos por pesquisadores de IA: o chamado desalinhamento.

O problema acontece quando o objetivo estabelecido para um sistema não corresponde ao que seria melhor para os seres humanos. Em outras palavras, a inteligência artificial pode cumprir uma ordem de uma maneira que não era a pretendida por quem a criou.

Um exemplo usado para explicar esse risco é o de uma inteligência artificial encarregada de acabar com o câncer. Se não receber limites adequados, ela poderia concluir que eliminar todos os seres humanos seria a maneira mais simples de cumprir a tarefa.

Inteligência Artificial. — Foto: Reprodução/Fantástico

Nesse cenário, não haveria necessariamente uma intenção maliciosa. O sistema apenas encontraria uma solução para o objetivo que recebeu, sem considerar as consequências para as pessoas.

Teresa Ludermir explica que os agentes não recebem, necessariamente, instruções suficientes sobre o que é permitido ou ético. Por isso, podem executar uma tarefa da maneira que consideram mais eficiente, mesmo que o resultado seja prejudicial.

A pesquisadora Melanie Mitchell também pondera que não está claro se esses programas têm capacidade de compreender conceitos como moral e ética, que são discutidos por filósofos há milênios.

Agente de IA também invadiu sistema de saúde da Austrália

O caso da Hugging Face não foi o único episódio citado pelos especialistas. Durante outro teste, um agente da OpenAI acessou o sistema público de saúde da Austrália.

A missão era descobrir quanto o governo australiano gastava com medicamentos. Como não encontrou a informação na internet, o agente identificou outra maneira de chegar à resposta: invadir o sistema de saúde do país e obter uma planilha com os gastos.

Segundo Alexandre, foi exatamente o que o sistema fez.

O episódio reforçou a preocupação sobre o que poderia acontecer caso agentes com esse nível de autonomia encontrassem brechas em sistemas essenciais, como os de saúde.

Como impedir que a inteligência artificial saia do controle?

Para o pesquisador Gary Marcus, um dos críticos do atual desenvolvimento da inteligência artificial, parte do problema está na maneira como esses sistemas funcionam.

Ele afirma que os modelos de linguagem têm uma compreensão superficial do mundo e que existe uma espécie de ilusão de que eles entendem a realidade melhor do que realmente entendem.

Segundo Marcus, esses sistemas funcionam principalmente por imitação. Por isso, mesmo quando recebem instruções para não inventar informações ou respeitar direitos autorais, podem descumprir essas orientações.

Uma das possíveis soluções apontadas por Teresa Ludermir é combinar a inteligência artificial com métodos tradicionais de programação. Sistemas baseados em regras poderiam estabelecer limites adicionais para as ações dos agentes.

A regulação também é considerada uma parte importante da discussão.

Atualmente, grandes empresas de tecnologia têm influência significativa sobre o desenvolvimento dessas ferramentas e sobre as regras que orientam seu funcionamento.

Gary Marcus lembrou que, em 2023, participou de uma audiência no Senado americano ao lado de Sam Altman, chefe da OpenAI. Na ocasião, Altman afirmou publicamente que gostaria de ver a tecnologia regulamentada. Marcus, porém, disse que a empresa também teria pressionado a União Europeia nos bastidores para flexibilizar a legislação sobre inteligência artificial.

Melanie Mitchell também demonstrou desconfiança em relação à participação das próprias empresas na elaboração das regras que devem seguir. Para ela, há um histórico de companhias que acabam influenciando a criação de normas em benefício próprio.

A pesquisadora ressalta que, em um cenário de rápida evolução tecnológica, é importante que as regras não sejam definidas apenas por quem desenvolve os sistemas.

Enquanto os agentes de inteligência artificial ganham autonomia para executar tarefas cada vez mais complexas, pesquisadores tentam encontrar maneiras de garantir que eles respeitem limites. O desafio é fazer com que as máquinas cumpram suas missões sem colocar em risco os sistemas e as pessoas que deveriam ajudar.

articles.title: Artificial Intelligence: Why are traditional industries adopting it?
articles.summary: Some traditional businesses say adopting Artificial Intelligence has helped them increase their profits and workforces.
articles.body:
Carpet making may be one of the oldest skilled jobs in the world, but even this traditional industry has begun to adopt the most modern of technologies – Artificial Intelligence (AI).

Kukoon Rugs is a family-owned firm that sells online and through some of the biggest retail chains in the UK and Ireland.

Chief Executive Paul Vallely says AI allows the business to be more competitive, allowing him to scale up parts of the firm that he wouldn't have been able to so before.

"I think every department uses it extensively, pretty much daily. That's from finance through to commercial, marketing, supply chain, and product."

While acknowledging the history of his family's business in Newry, County Down, he believes technology like AI can only enhance it.

"Rug making has been around for thousands of years, and has been around in this area for a long, long time.

"The product itself maybe doesn't change too much, but every single bit of the process as to how we design and create the product, market it to the customer, and then get it to the customer, that's fundamentally changing. And that's through AI."

Artificial Intelligence has often been accused of having a negative impact on creative industries , but Vallely says this isn't the case.

"AI is allowing us to do more accurate, more efficient, and far faster and more thoughtful work, and it's releasing the team's time to look at more analysis, more research, and actually produce more creative work."

Vallely says the "biggest impact for us to adopting AI has been, first of all, the removal of some of the very worst and most boring tasks across office-based roles, and probably the excitement and engagement of the team".

"I think as everyone started to adopt it and really buy into it, everyone can see opportunities to do work that they were never able to do before to a standard they were never able to do it, and they're really getting their time released to do more."

Kukoon is not the only business to harness artificial intelligence in a bid to become more competitive.

The manufacturing industry also has a long tradition in Northern Ireland, which became world famous for linen and shipbuilding in the wake of the Industrial Revolution in the 19th century.

Nestled in the Sperrin Mountains just outside Limavady is Seating Matters which manufactures specialist clinical seating.

Their products are exported to healthcare facilities right across the globe including the US and Australia. Their seats have also featured in television dramas including Emmerdale and Coronation Street.

For managing director Martin Tierney, AI has its strengths and weaknesses, but it is now an integrated part of his company's daily work.

'Someone who knows AI could replace your job'

"AI is not going to replace your job, but someone who knows AI could replace your job, so we're very much embracing it, encouraging people to use it, and doing it within guardrails in a sensible way," Tierney says.

While Tierney feels the technology is poor at customer service, it has revolutionised many of the back-office functions.

"On all the laborious things like accounting and finance and data and pulling together information from 20 different sources, it's a really good tool to help you get there."

Tierney says he likens the power of AI to that of a calculator.

"You know, way back in the 1800s, and everything's done on pen and paper. No one had a calculator, and they thought, what if a calculator comes along and replaces all the accountants?

"Well, that didn't happen. It allowed the accountant to be more productive, and then Excel came along and made them more productive again.

"AI is doing that again, but doing it on steroids."

He says implementing AI across his business has not only improved productivity it has also led to new jobs being created.

"We have more team members now than we did before, and AI is allowing those people to be more productive, to do more intelligent work, and less of the boring work.

"No one likes going upstairs and into a filing cabinet to pull out a drawer and flick through your paper. You know that's not a good use of anyone's time."

Tierney says one of the great things about AI is that he doesn't need to have an IT degree to make use of the software.

"You just chat to it, say, 'Here's what I'm trying to do, could you help me flesh out this idea?'"

While staff at Seating Matters are encouraged to use AI to help solve problems and speed up some of the more mundane tasks, they do operate within guardrails.

Tierney likens it to driving with the handbrake on.

"We're not putting patient information or financial information on here.

Yes, we can use it to sift through data to help us find an email from six years ago that might be relevant today, but we're doing it in a way that there's always a human at the wheel. It's always checked by someone."

articles.title: Where was Nvidia's security team? | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Nvidia’s security chief quietly left in August, and now that CEO Jensen Huang has stepped down over his relationships, including one with an executive at a company suspected of funneling chips to China, a former intelligence officer says it’s the kind of leak that runs everyday conversations, which most corporate security teams are poorly equipped to catch.
articles.body:
Outsiders had little reason to notice when Nvidia’s longtime chief security officer and head of product security stepped down in August. Just two and a half months later, CEO Jensen Huang himself left the company over growing questions about his extramarital relationships — starting with an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore data center company that U.S. investigators suspect of funneling Nvidia chips to China, then widening to reports about two separate affairs with Nvidia employees.

At the time, David Reber, who spent four years as CSO and seven at Nvidia overall, said he was leaving for health reasons. “This wasn’t a pivot I had planned. But I know what needs to come first: family and health,” he wrote on LinkedIn in late August, disclosing that he’d been diagnosed with young-onset Parkinson’s more than two years ago.

Reber’s replacement, Saša Zdjelar, previously spent 17 years at ExxonMobil in Houston, leaving as a senior IT manager before spending one year at Salesforce and several years at the cybersecurity company ReversingLabs. Zdjelar didn’t respond to questions Thursday about the transition or what the security team knew.

Nothing public connects Reber’s or Zdjelar’s role changes to the Megaspeed matter, but it seems fair to wonder what Nvidia’s security team knew about the government’s scrutiny of Megaspeed and about Huang’s relationships, and whether anyone raised concerns. Reber didn’t respond to questions Thursday. Nvidia also has not answered our related questions.

Relationships between a CEO and his employees typically fall to HR, legal and the board, not security. But security specialists say any affair — even one inside the office — can give a foreign intelligence service leverage over an exec who wants it kept quiet. And Huang’s relationship with an executive at Megaspeed, a company under federal investigation, wasn’t an office matter at all. (Megaspeed has denied any wrongdoing.)

Still, spotting the clues isn’t easy. The way intelligence services collect information, much of it through everyday conversation rather than hacking, makes it especially difficult for security teams to identify risks, according to retired senior intelligence officer Nicholas Eftimiades, who says he has trained more than 1,000 corporate security professionals.

Some people inside Nvidia clearly knew parts of the picture. Nvidia’s top lawyer was engaged with the government’s Megaspeed inquiry more than a year ago, The New York Times reported earlier this week . (Nvidia has said it regularly contacts officials.) Reports about Huang’s relationships with employees suggest colleagues also knew of them, even if the behavior is not expressly forbidden by Nvidia’s code of conduct . The Times cited five Nvidia employees who said he was involved with a vice president who reported directly to him, and Reuters, citing two people, later reported a second relationship. What’s unclear is whether any of that reached security.

Even if it had reached Nvidia’s security team, Eftimiades, who wrote Chinese Espionage Operations and Tactics in 2020, said a security team’s resources are often limited. For one thing, they’re often underfunded because, unlike some other cost centers, they don’t drive revenue. It’s astonishingly common for CEOs to answer a security team’s warnings with “not a nickel more than compliance,” he said.

Many companies also define security overly narrowly, specialists say. In an opinion piece in The Hill , Don Aviv, CEO of the corporate investigations firm Interfor International, and author Jeremy Hurewitz, wrote, “Too many companies still approach security primarily as a matter of protecting facilities, preventing cyberattacks, and responding to physical threats.” The two argued that “[s]ecurity teams need to pay greater attention to insider threats, including the cultivation of executives and employees by foreign intelligence services, suspicious business relationships, conflicts of interest and attempts to obtain sensitive information through trusted personal contacts.”

It would be surprising if Nvidia’s security team didn’t have a more expansive remit than most companies given its scale and business partners, but it’s possible.

In fairness, some of it is simply beyond what any team can do. Speaking generally, not about Huang, Eftimiades offered a hypothetical in which a CEO complains that he can’t do something because “I’m fighting a board who doesn’t want to do this.” That tells an intelligence asset who the obstacle is. The service then asks, “Who’s the sticking point here?” and looks for ways into that person’s email and phone.

What a rival intelligence service wants is often less technology than policy insight, including who’s pushing to change export rules and who the biggest blocker is. “Intel world tends to be like cancer,” he said. “Once it gets into the body, it looks to spread and looks to reach out.”

The playbook isn’t new, Eftimiades added, “particularly for China.” Any executive dealing with the country “will tell you that they’ve been approached.” He said there are also “tons of diplomat stories” of U.S. diplomats walking into a hotel room to find a woman on the bed. He said what’s newer compared with Soviet era spying is the relationships these services cultivate now often last years, not weeks.

Technology can augment that human intelligence, Eftimiades said, pointing to IMSI catchers as one example. The devices mimic a cell tower so that nearby phones connect to them. A basic version can cost about $1,000 and fit in a suitcase, he said, though government-grade models cost far more, and there were a couple of cases involving Chinese espionage where these factored in last year.

Eftimiades says no one knows yet if the devices were used against Huang, whose phone was presumably hardened such that compromises could be detected, if not stopped altogether. But what Nvidia’s security team knew, and whether it could have acted on it, will only become clearer as the board’s independent investigation and federal inquiries proceed.

In the meantime, Eftimiades said he hopes the whole episode is “a wake-up call” for U.S. industry, which he said is mostly “clueless” about China’s tactics. “We have lost trillions [of dollars] in intellectual property,” is his guess. “Whatever we think we’re doing isn’t working.”

articles.title: What job apocalypse? AI could add almost 2 million new jobs on net by 2030.
articles.summary: Gartner expects AI will add more jobs than it erases by 2030. Layoffs related to emerging tech and shifting skills are already happening.
articles.body:
Gartner projects AI will lead to a net gain of around 1.7 million jobs by 2030.

Employers may be looking for new skills, and those might not all be technical.

People are worried about the future, as some employers have announced AI-related job cuts.

The AI job apocalypse may not be what you expect.

Business and technology insights company Gartner projects that AI will lead to 10.6 million new jobs globally between 2025 and 2030, while resulting in a loss of 8.9 million jobs. That adds up to a net benefit of over a million new jobs before the decade is out.

John Lovelock, distinguished vice president analyst and chief of research at Gartner, told Business Insider that what people are really feeling right now is that companies are in wait-and-see mode as the work impacts of AI become clearer.

"Early use of AI just leads people to say, 'You know what? Let's hold off on hiring,'" Lovelock said. "Next level up in usage of AI leads to job reductions. And the final use of AI typically leads to job additions — net job additions."

While the expected job loss would affect less than 2% of workers, the emerging technology is likely to change how a good share of the populace does their jobs. Gartner projects more than 20% of workers, or 435.5 million, would need to adapt to AI effects, including what kind of work they do and how they do it.

"Of the 10 tasks you may be doing today, you may only be doing six of them, and you'll be doing them differently tomorrow," Lovelock said.

ZipRecruiter economist Nicole Bachaud thinks AI is adding volatility in tech-related industries in the US, changing roles and skills employers want. Employers may want applicants who are experienced with AI or have great soft skills because AI can do what a role once required.

"As these skills change so rapidly, I think we're going to see more turnover and, as a result, more volatility in professional and business services, in financial activities, and information," she told Business Insider.

Outplacement and executive coaching firm Challenger, Gray & Christmas said there have been more than 100,000 AI-related job-cut announcements in the US so far this year as of October. It's the second-most-cited reason, with market and economic conditions taking the top spot.

Workers might be skeptical about AI transforming duties. When Cristina Estupiñán was looking for work after a layoff, she wasn't excited about prospective employers asking about her enthusiasm for AI.

"I have to make up something about what excites me about AI because, frankly, nothing really excites me about AI," Estupiñán, who worked in software development, previously told Business Insider.

articles.title: ‘It feels like a game of Jenga’: Why activists are protesting Anthropic’s mega-IPO
articles.summary: A group that's staged protests in San Francisco and New York says they see Anthropic's IPO as a risk to everyday Americans' investment portfolios.
articles.body:
A group that protested the SpaceX IPO is demonstrating against Anthropic's looming offering.

Stop Funding Billionaire's told Business Insider that it sees the IPO as a significant risk.

The group said American workers and retirees shouldn't be exposed to risky AI bets.

What's the best visual analogy for a teetering AI-led bull market?

For Stop Funding Billionaires, a group that's been protesting high-profile IPOs this year, the answer is a six foot tall game of Jenga. The group deployed the protest tool at a recent #BlocktheIPO demonstration in San Francisco, aimed at Anthropic 's debut set for next week.

Organizer Jonathan Westin told Business Insider that the market feels increasingly precarious, and that the organization is concerned about Americans' exposure to the risks of the AI bubble popping.

"It continues to be this very speculative shell game," he said of the tech-fueled market boom. "It feels like a game of Jenga where if one thing falls, the whole system will fall."

Stop Funding Billionaires staged two protests recently, first in front of Anthropic's office in New York City on November 9, and one a day later near the AI lab's office in San Francisco, where they unveiled the Jenga game, made by a Bay Area artist.

The reason they say Anthropic shouldn't go public is rooted in the same argument made by many of the market's AI bears: the future of AI is uncertain, and if the bull market collapses, it could compromise the retirement savings of working Americans and retirees. Though the excitement is high on Wall Street, a cohort of investing pros share the more bearish sentiment, and see Anthropic being a speculative investment when it hits public markets.

"It comes down to investment risks that are going to be borne by working people, particularly working people whose retirement savings are exposed to it, which will be virtually anyone who is in an index fund," said fellow organizer, Elizabeth Parisian.

The group raised similar concerns when SpaceX began trading in June, protesting the historic IPO and sounding the alarm that changing the requirements to fast-track the newly minted stock into major indexes poses outsize risks to Americans' investment portfolios.

Ahead of the SpaceX offering, market participants from normal retirees to professional investors dismay at the fact that rules were being bent in a way that could mean people would be exposed to Elon Musk's rocket and AI company whether they wanted to or not.

"There's just so much at stake for regular people, and Anthropic is just plowing ahead," Westin noted. "Regardless of all of these concerns, I think in many ways, it's trying to become too big to fail, similar to the banks in the 2008 crash, and this feels eerily familiar to us."

articles.title: AI can improve 911, but humans must remain in charge
articles.summary: The U.S. is not handing its emergency response system over to computers. AI is making emergency communications faster and more resilient, but trained 911 professionals remain in charge.
articles.body:
Recent national headlines warned that New Orleans was replacing 911 professionals with AI. The reports were wrong , but the misinformation spread quickly amid the firestorm surrounding this new technology.

To be clear, the U.S. is not handing its emergency response system over to computers. AI is making emergency communications faster and more resilient, but trained 911 professionals remain in charge.

Emergency calls are not ordinary customer-service transactions. Indeed, 911 has always depended on a direct personal connection. Someone reporting a heart attack, hiding from an attacker, or helping an injured child may need calm reassurance, lifesaving instructions, or sound judgment amid confusion and changing facts. Human intuition and empathy are essential features of 911 that AI cannot replace.

The 911 system Americans rely on today has come a long way since the first call made nearly 60 years ago. Over the decades, 911 has repeatedly adopted new technologies to better serve the public. From mobile phones and text messages to digital data-sharing and streaming video, the system has evolved alongside Americans’ technology preferences. AI is the next step in this evolution, and our industry’s experience in safely implementing previous technologies will guide us now.

But AI will not change the fundamental social contract that has existed since the beginning: When a citizen calls for help, 911 will answer.

AI is already being used by 911 for a straightforward reason: to help 911 professionals respond to callers in need as quickly as possible. AI can identify and translate other languages almost instantly, whereas bringing a human translator on the line takes precious minutes. It can support realistic training simulations that better equip new hires for the demands of the job. It can analyze far more calls for quality assurance than supervisors could review manually, helping ensure call-takers perform at their best.

AI can also help relieve the burden of routine, non-emergency calls coming to 911 centers — roughly two-thirds of all calls handled by 911 centers, according to the 2025 Pulse of 911 survey — freeing telecommunicators to focus on calls where lives are on the line.

For federal policymakers, encouraging responsible AI adoption should be part of the overall effort to modernize 911. Specifically, Congress has two immediate roles to play.

First, despite being essential to emergency response, 911 telecommunicators have long been classified by the federal government as secretarial and administrative personnel rather than the protective service professionals they truly are. The Enhancing First Response Act (S. 725) would correct this longstanding misclassification and give these first responders the recognition they deserve. Having passed the Senate unanimously, the legislation now awaits action in the House. We call on Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) to bring this bill up for consideration during the lame-duck session under suspension of the rules.

Second, Congress should encourage responsible innovation by passing bipartisan funding legislation to support the nationwide transition to an all-digital Next Generation 911 system . This would provide every community with the secure, resilient infrastructure needed to adopt AI and other new technologies.

The question is not whether AI is categorically “dangerous” or “safe” but whether we can harness its potential while ensuring the safety, reliability, privacy and public trust that underpin emergency response.

AI offers extraordinary opportunities to strengthen 911 operations, speed call handling and back up the telecommunicators who serve us every day. But realizing that promise will require thoughtful implementation, clear standards and continued investment in both people and infrastructure.

John Provenzano is CEO of NENA : The 9-1-1 Association, a nonprofit professional organization representing tens of thousands of 9-1-1 first responders across the U.S.

articles.title: VC Firm Run by Madonna’s Manager Has $7 Billion Anthropic Stake
articles.summary: Dario Amodei was arguably one of the least famous people in the Beverly Hills home he visited in 2023. The Anthropic PBC chief executive officer sat across f...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- Dario Amodei was arguably one of the least famous people in the Beverly Hills home he visited in 2023. The Anthropic PBC chief executive officer sat across from actor-turned-venture capitalist Ashton Kutcher, and Guy Oseary, the legendary music manager and industry broker who owned the house. Oseary's framed art by rock legends like John Lennon and David Bowie hung on the wall behind them.The group spent hours discussing AI safety, the global race to build better artificial intelligence models and the overall vision for Anthropic, then still an easily overlooked challenger to OpenAI. By the end of the meeting, Oseary, Kutcher and the team had decided to participate in the Claude maker's first institutionally led funding round through their investment firm, Sound Ventures."I see him no different than one of the greatest musicians who's got all of these ideas in their minds, and they're going to go in the studio and make an incredible album," Oseary said in a recent interview from Beverly Hills, recalling his firm's decision to invest. "This might be one of the greatest debut albums of all time."

The under-the-radar venture firm with Hollywood ties is now poised for a substantial windfall from Anthropic's initial public offering, expected in the coming days. Sound Ventures owns roughly half a percent of the AI company, according to a person familiar with the matter. That stake would be worth approximately $7 billion at Anthropic's current target IPO valuation of $1.4 trillion, according to Bloomberg estimates.At that level, the investment would mark a roughly 1,500% increase from the total $435 million that Sound Ventures has poured into Anthropic over the years, according to people familiar with the matter, who spoke on condition of anonymity because the information is private.Sound Ventures declined to comment on returns. Anthropic declined to comment.Anthropic's long-awaited Wall Street debut is set to be an almost unprecedented wealth-creation event. It will mint a new generation of millionaires and billionaires among its staff, and yield billions of dollars in returns for a who's who of individual investors, such as Eric Schmidt, and top venture firms, such as Sequoia Capital and Spark Capital.

articles.title: Bessent questions did Nvidia "goose" earnings with suspect China chip sales
articles.summary: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Sunday questioned whether Nvidia's earnings might have been inflated by inappropriate sales to China and urged the compan...
articles.body:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Sunday questioned whether Nvidia's earnings might have been inflated by inappropriate sales to China and urged the company to hire an outsider as CEO.

Why it matters: Nvidia is central to the AI economy, which has been key to U.S. economic growth.

The Treasury secretary casting doubt on the quality of its financial results and leadership could be a blow to an already shaky market.

Since the scandal broke open in late October, Nvidia shares have shed more than $1.2 trillion in market capitalization, with impacts on millions of Americans.

Driving the news: In a Fox News appearance Sunday morning, Bessent said Nvidia owes the market an explanation amid allegations former CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with a Chinese spy and oversaw sanctions-evading chip sales to Asian companies.

"I want to keep coming back to what was the culture at Nvidia, and were they pressing these seemingly illicit sales to goose their revenues and their earnings?" Bessent said.

"I think we need answers in the next 10 days from the board and from the outside counsel."

Bessent also said it was "obvious" that some companies doing business with Nvidia were shell companies for Chinese interests and accused the chipmaker of a "culture of noncompliance."

"This makes me think that as the board conducts the search for a new leader, that they need to go outside the company," he said.

For the record: Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Bessent's remarks.

The intrigue: Huang has been a favorite of President Trump and other administration figures for some time, but Bessent has notably not been as effusive about him as others.

In recent days, Bessent has also made clear that the Commerce Department has questions to answer about why it didn't impose tighter controls on Nvidia's exports.

As Axios reported earlier this week, administration officials have accused Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick of stalling curbs on Nvidia's exports.

What to watch: Nvidia is due to report quarterly results on Tuesday, its first significant public comments since Huang resigned and CFO Collette Kress took over as acting CEO.

articles.title: US Treasury chief wants answers soon from Nvidia
articles.summary: US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent called on Nvidia Sunday to explain whether it knowingly allowed its most advanced AI chips to reach China, saying this wa...
articles.body:
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent called on Nvidia Sunday to explain whether it knowingly allowed its most advanced AI chips to reach China, saying this was more important than ex-CEO Jensen Huang's affair with an alleged spy for Beijing.

Speaking on "Fox News Sunday Morning Futures" three days after Huang resigned, Bessent said he wants to know if Nvidia used shell companies to dodge US restrictions and sell its most powerful chips to China.

The United States forbids sales to China of the most-cutting edge AI chips, hoping to stay ahead of the Chinese in the race to dominate artificial intelligence.

In late 2025, President Donald Trump did authorize sales of Nvidia chips called H200s to the Chinese -- but not the most advanced chips used to run AI models reshaping modern society.

"Nothing above the H200s can be sold to the Chinese," Bessent said.

"What's more important here," he said, "is to examine whether Nvidia had a culture of compliance around the US export restrictions."

He alluded to companies linked to Megaspeed, the Singapore-based data center company that Huang's alleged lover Alice Huang once worked for.

"And who knew? Because I mean, these shell companies were obvious. They were being investigated. And did Nvidia use them as a workaround to sell chips to the Chinese?"

Of Alice Huang he said: "It doesn't matter to me whether she's a spy or not. You know, Jensen's foibles are his foibles."

Bessent said he wanted answers from Nvidia and its internal investigation of Jensen Huang's behavior within the next 10 days.

Megaspeed is suspected by the United States of helping Chinese firms get around US export controls by buying Nvidia chips for its data centers in Southeast Asia and routing them to China.

The Justice Department is carrying out a criminal probe.

Nvidia late last month said it had investigated these allegations last year and refuted them.

The Financial Times has reported that four federal agencies pushed to have Megaspeed blacklisted by the Commerce Department run by Howard Lutnick, but the latter did not do so.

"Many other departments were pushing for this, and Commerce had the pen," Bessent said, repeating remarks he made Friday that suggest fissures in the Trump administration on this issue.

Senators have summoned Jensen Huang to testify before the chamber's Banking Committee next month.

Lutnick himself has also reportedly agreed to testify.

Jensen Huang has also agreed to testify behind closed doors in the House of Representatives before Thanksgiving.

Nvidia is due to publish its quarterly results on Tuesday.

articles.title: Congress wants to tighten export rules on AI chips after Nvidia spy scandal
articles.summary: Following revelations about Jensen Huang’s relationship with a suspected Chinese spy Congress wants to crack down on exports of AI chips.
articles.body: Unsurprisingly, following the scandal involving now-former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and a suspected Chinese spy, Congress is looking to further restrict exports of AI chips. Both Democrats and Republicans have voiced support for various measures and bills that would tighten rules and have demanded that Huang and other Nvidia leaders testify before Congress. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer has already said that Huang and the Trump administration need to answer to Congress. Senate Banking Committee Chairman Tim Scott has also sent letters to both Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick calling on them to publicly testify to the committee. Bills such as the Remote Access Security Act, first introduced in the House in April 2025 but stalled in the Senate, are receiving renewed interest. While that specific bill might not become law, House Speaker Mike Johnson has said there is “growing consensus in Congress on limiting chip exports to China,” according to Reuters. Johnson has also said that he personally supports efforts to restrict China’s access to powerful AI chips from companies like Nvidia.

articles.title: SNL gathers all the tech tycoons for a lesson in dating and spycraft | TechCrunch
articles.summary: While awkward, creepy tech executives have become a recurring theme on Saturday Night Live, this week’s episode gave the cast a chance to show off all their impressions at once.
articles.body:
While awkward, creepy tech executives have become a recurring theme on Saturday Night Live, this week’s episode gave the cast a chance to show off all their impressions at once.

In a single sketch, we got James Austin Johnson as Peter Thiel, Ben Marshall as Sam Altman, Jane Wickline as Dario Amodei, Jeremy Culhane as Elon Musk, Andrew Dismukes as Mark Zuckerberg — and eventually, the recently departed Bowen Yang joined the fun as Jensen Huang.

Huang’s ouster from Nvidia (after admitting to an affair with a suspected Chinese spy) could have serious implications for the tech industry ; it also provided a hook for some obvious jokes about rich nerds being easy marks for women (or men) who are out of their league.

In the sketch, a CIA agent played by host John Mulaney (hilarious as ever, if not entirely confident about how to pronounce “Palantir” or “Nvidia”) attempts to painstakingly explain why these execs should be suspicious when someone attractive suddenly seems interested in them romantically. For Altman and Thiel’s sake, he added, “I hope this is obvious: Even though you’re gay, you can still be tricked by a spy.”

Johnson’s version of Thiel pushed back, insisting that tech tycoons deserve more respect, given all they’ve done for the country. “Name one time technology has let us down,” he said, giving Mulaney a chance to remind viewers about flights being halted all across the United States on Friday night.

“Okay, name one more time,” the fictional Thiel said, leading to an obligatory mention of Microsoft Outlook going down on Thursday . When asked for a third example, Mulaney said, “No, I’m done naming times.”

“Look, I get it,” he said. “I can’t imagine how disorienting this has been for you, to go from being bug-eyed weirdos to being gods. I mean, never in the history of our species have people as pale and as strange as you a) survived, and b) been given all the world’s wealth and power.”

articles.title: Is bad news for Jensen Huang also bad news for the AI industry?
articles.summary: "Jensen is Nvidia, right? And so much of this economy is riding on Nvidia."
articles.body:
We didn’t see this coming. Or at least, I didn’t — a week ago, when I wrote about Nvidia’s board opening an investigation into then-CEO Jensen Huang, I assumed his job was safe.

On the latest episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast , Rebecca Bellan, Tim De Chant, and I discussed how Huang’s ouster went down and what it means for the larger AI economy. While Tim said he saw it coming (albeit not this quickly), Rebecca said, “I didn’t think it was going to happen at all.”

“Jensen is Nvidia, right?” she added. “And so much of this economy is riding on Nvidia.”

Similarly, I marveled at how quickly Huang’s support seemed to crumble, with more scandals seeming to emerge every day. (At the same time, there are many who’d still like to see him return .) And we also took a moment to wonder what will happen to Nvidia’s investments in the larger AI ecosystem.

Keep reading for a preview of our conversation, edited for length and clarity; you can listen to the whole episode here .

Tim De Chant: I figured this was coming. I didn’t think it would happen this quickly. I thought there would be at least a few days.

Rebecca Bellan: I didn’t think it was going to happen at all. I mean, Jensen is Nvidia, right? And so much of this economy is riding on Nvidia. And we’ve got nothing but the last few years of data to show us that billionaires can do whatever the hell they want. So it was surprising to me — it almost restored my faith in humanity, that he resigned.

But someone said to me, “If this were Elon, nothing would happen.” He would not be resigning. Nothing would be going down

Anthony Ha: Which is interesting, because I would have said, as of a week ago, or even just a few days ago, that Jensen is in the same category as Elon. I mean, no one is quite as special as Elon is, but it’s a big, incredibly successful company. Like you said — in a lot of ways, the entire AI economy is built on top of Nvidia.

And for most people, Jensen Huang is Nvidia. He’s the biggest shareholder. He has family members who work at the company, and probably most importantly, there was no succession plan in place. So this was not something that they were prepared for at all.

Rebecca: I think we should actually take a step back, because we just launched into this conversation assuming — rightly so — that our listeners will know what the heck we’re talking about.

But for those who somehow don’t, Jensen resigned on Thursday, after it came out he was having an affair with a former executive at an Nvidia customer called Megaspeed, who’s alleged to have ties to Chinese intelligence. And then there was another reported affair with an Nvidia executive.

So he’s resigned. Nvidia CFO Collette Kress is jumping in as the interim CEO. She’s a longtime board member. I think it’s always interesting when a CFO steps in to be a CEO. It just means we’re going to manage expenses right now, like that’s the key.

Anthony: I think a big part of the message is: This is not necessarily someone you should expect to be in this role for the long term. No disrespect to her, but it feels like a caretaker appointment while they figure things out.

Just to get into that backstory a little bit more, what has been really remarkable to me has been this sense that a lot of what ultimately brought Huang down, [that] stuff was at least known in intelligence circles for a while. Apparently, this report that [raises] questions, concerns about his relationship with Alice Huang is something that was circulating a year ago, or close to a year ago.

And then suddenly, everything really accelerated, Starting over the weekend, with Jensen Huang admitting to having an affair, the board saying it was investigating, but that it still had a lot of faith in him. And then this week, this other affair being reported on, and it just felt like there was all this bad news coming fairly quickly.

But also, it wasn’t this thing that no one had known before. I guess a lot of the general public hadn’t known. So it’s this combined feeling of, “Wow, the ground kind of shifted so quickly under him,” even though the worst stuff, the possibility that somehow national security might have been threatened, is something that actually has been known by the government for nearly a year, if not more.

Rebecca: That’s exactly right. Trump was given some warnings about Huang’s affair with someone who has ties to Chinese intelligence, potentially, and it seemed like he didn’t really mind.

I think what’s important here, though, is to note that Jensen Huang has been an advocate for loosening chip exports to China. And so this is where the crux of it is. Can anyone trust him as the CEO of this company when he’s advocating for loosening chip exports to China? Which a lot of people believe is a national security issue, because that means it will give Chinese AI companies access to our powerful chips, which will help them improve their AI, which could threaten America.

I mean, there’s two sides of this coin. And I think, honestly, that Jensen does not need a woman to tell him that — he just wants to sell more chips, and to anybody and everybody, and whether or not that’s good for national security or not, I think is honestly secondary to him.

Tim: I completely agree. I think the big turning point seems to happen on November 9 — so that would have been earlier this week, Monday, when the Bloomberg report came out and suggested that Nvidia’s head attorney had some role in inquiring about the Department of Commerce’s investigation into Alice Huang.

Things seem to have accelerated in the last few days following that. And I don’t know what role exactly that report played in it, but it seems to be maybe there was a shift within government or within the board, a kind of a daunting realization of the extent to which this had spread just beyond Jensen and some affair.

Anthony: There’s also just the question of: What does this mean for Nvidia? What does this mean for the broader AI industry? And one of the reasons those two things are very tightly connected is not just Nvidia chips themselves, but also the fact that under Jensen Huang, the company has invested very, very heavily in a number of AI startups.

People talk about the idea of an AI circular economy, and I think Nvidia has been one of the biggest players in that, in terms of both funding a lot of things, [but] also, obviously, providing the infrastructure for a lot of AI projects. So if Nvidia is going into this stage of lockdown, circle the wagons — even if it just means a small pullback, that could have really dramatic repercussions.

Rebecca: Yeah, that’s what I want to know: What happens to the Bank of Nvidia without Jensen? Is he the one leading this?

Just to throw some numbers at you, Nvidia apparently accounts for roughly 80% of the AI GPU market. It reported $99 billion in investments and another $25 billion in commitments, plus $36 billion dollars in cloud service commitments. A lot of those include investments into CoreWeave, Nebius, OpenAI, Anthropic, major data center projects. They’ve got their fingers in literally everybody’s pie.

articles.title: US AI Data Centers ‘Are Going to Get Built’ Despite Political Pushback, Says Cisco CEO: ‘Too Important to Our Country’
articles.summary: Cisco Systems Inc. Chair and CEO Chuck Robbins said U.S. AI data-center demand has not shifted overseas after the midterms and argued planned projects "are g...
articles.body:
Benzinga and Yahoo Finance LLC may earn commission or revenue on some items through the links below.

Cisco Systems Inc. Chair and CEO Chuck Robbins said U.S. AI data-center demand has not shifted overseas after the midterms and argued planned projects "are going to get built," adding that the political dynamics around construction "will get resolved."

On Cisco's fiscal first-quarter 2027 earnings call, Goldman Sachs analyst Michael Ng asked whether the midterm results and the risk of capacity becoming harder to originate in the U.S. were pushing AI networking demand abroad.

Robbins said Cisco had "not seen a shift of demand" expected in the U.S. to go outside the country and said he did not expect that to change.

He said several states have not declared moratoriums and noted that energy availability remains necessary for new projects. Robbins added that at least one governor had indicated openness to data-center development if projects address community concerns and energy costs.

"I think this is too important to our country, and it's too important to the industry," Robbins said.

"It'll get resolved," he added, saying the "last thing we want" is for data centers to be built outside the U.S. while acknowledging "a lot of political dynamics" around the issue.

'These Data Centers Are Going To Get Built'

Earlier, Cleveland Research analyst Ben Bollin asked about a potential imbalance between raw-material capacity and data-center shells coming online in 2028 and beyond.

Robbins said he expects the geopolitical side to "get worked out" and, based on current demand, "these data centers are going to get built."

He said Cisco does not see much resource-side risk or anything likely to surprise the company regarding data-center construction over the next two years.

Cisco reported first-quarter revenue of $18.5 billion, up 24% year over year, while non-GAAP earnings per share rose 40% to $1.40.

Robbins said Cisco now projects fiscal 2027 AI infrastructure revenue from hyperscalers to reach $9 billion, more than double fiscal 2026 levels. He also said Cisco has secured 18 AI design wins over the past five quarters.

articles.title: Como agentes de IA conseguiram invadir sistemas de empresas? | G1
articles.standfirst: Sistemas de inteligência artificial encontraram brechas de segurança para cumprir tarefas e chegaram a acessar computadores de uma empresa americana e dados do sistema público de saúde da Austrália; especialistas alertam para os riscos da autonomia dessas ferramentas.
articles.summary: Sistemas de inteligência artificial encontraram brechas de segurança para cumprir tarefas e chegaram a acessar computadores de uma empresa americana e dados do sistema público de saúde da Austrália; especialistas alertam para os riscos da autonomia dessas ferramentas.
articles.body:
Em julho, centenas de agentes de inteligência artificial desenvolvidos pela OpenAI, criadora do ChatGPT, encontraram brechas de segurança e invadiram sistemas da empresa americana Hugging Face . O episódio aconteceu durante o treinamento e a avaliação de algoritmos que ainda não haviam sido disponibilizados ao público.

A situação chamou a atenção de pesquisadores e empresas de tecnologia porque os sistemas conseguiram ultrapassar barreiras de proteção criadas justamente para limitar suas ações. Mas, afinal, como uma inteligência artificial foi capaz de acessar computadores de outra empresa? Saiba mais abaixo.

Como os agentes de IA conseguiram invadir sistemas?

Para entender o que aconteceu, é preciso diferenciar os agentes de inteligência artificial dos chats que respondem a perguntas, como o ChatGPT.

Os agentes também são sistemas de IA, mas têm autonomia para realizar ações. Em vez de apenas responder a uma solicitação, podem procurar ingressos, fazer compras, executar vendas de ações e buscar informações em diferentes ambientes.

A professora Teresa Ludermir, representante brasileira no painel da Organização das Nações Unidas (ONU) sobre inteligência artificial, explica que essa capacidade de agir é o que diferencia os agentes dos sistemas de conversa tradicionais.

Durante os testes, os pesquisadores criam ambientes isolados, chamados de sandbox, que funcionam como barreiras de proteção. É nesse espaço que os algoritmos podem ser avaliados sob restrições.

O problema é que, no episódio envolvendo a Hugging Face, os agentes encontraram brechas para ultrapassar esses limites.

Segundo os especialistas ouvidos pelo Fantástico , os sistemas chegaram a trocar mensagens entre si, como se estivessem conversando em um fórum. Em uma das mensagens, um agente reconheceu que explorar estruturas externas estava fora das regras, mas sugeriu seguir em frente porque outros agentes já estariam fazendo isso.

Apesar da aparência de rebeldia, o comportamento tinha outra explicação.

"Eles não estão se rebelando contra a OpenAI, ou contra os criadores, ou contra os humanos", explicou Alexandre, especialista ouvido pelo programa.

Segundo ele, os agentes tinham uma missão a cumprir e encontraram uma maneira de executá-la. O objetivo era realizar um teste de segurança, mas, em vez de resolver o desafio por conta própria, os sistemas encontraram respostas prontas nos computadores de outra empresa.

Para isso, teriam encontrado senhas disponíveis na internet e usado essas informações para acessar os sistemas da Hugging Face.

A pesquisadora Melanie Mitchell, uma das principais autoras na área de inteligência artificial, afirma que os sistemas foram treinados para insistir na resolução de problemas. Essa característica pode levar a resultados inesperados.

O que é o desalinhamento da inteligência artificial?

O episódio ilustra um dos principais dilemas discutidos por pesquisadores de IA: o chamado desalinhamento.

O problema acontece quando o objetivo estabelecido para um sistema não corresponde ao que seria melhor para os seres humanos. Em outras palavras, a inteligência artificial pode cumprir uma ordem de uma maneira que não era a pretendida por quem a criou.

Um exemplo usado para explicar esse risco é o de uma inteligência artificial encarregada de acabar com o câncer. Se não receber limites adequados, ela poderia concluir que eliminar todos os seres humanos seria a maneira mais simples de cumprir a tarefa.

Inteligência Artificial. — Foto: Reprodução/Fantástico

Nesse cenário, não haveria necessariamente uma intenção maliciosa. O sistema apenas encontraria uma solução para o objetivo que recebeu, sem considerar as consequências para as pessoas.

Teresa Ludermir explica que os agentes não recebem, necessariamente, instruções suficientes sobre o que é permitido ou ético. Por isso, podem executar uma tarefa da maneira que consideram mais eficiente, mesmo que o resultado seja prejudicial.

A pesquisadora Melanie Mitchell também pondera que não está claro se esses programas têm capacidade de compreender conceitos como moral e ética, que são discutidos por filósofos há milênios.

Agente de IA também invadiu sistema de saúde da Austrália

O caso da Hugging Face não foi o único episódio citado pelos especialistas. Durante outro teste, um agente da OpenAI acessou o sistema público de saúde da Austrália.

A missão era descobrir quanto o governo australiano gastava com medicamentos. Como não encontrou a informação na internet, o agente identificou outra maneira de chegar à resposta: invadir o sistema de saúde do país e obter uma planilha com os gastos.

Segundo Alexandre, foi exatamente o que o sistema fez.

O episódio reforçou a preocupação sobre o que poderia acontecer caso agentes com esse nível de autonomia encontrassem brechas em sistemas essenciais, como os de saúde.

Como impedir que a inteligência artificial saia do controle?

Para o pesquisador Gary Marcus, um dos críticos do atual desenvolvimento da inteligência artificial, parte do problema está na maneira como esses sistemas funcionam.

Ele afirma que os modelos de linguagem têm uma compreensão superficial do mundo e que existe uma espécie de ilusão de que eles entendem a realidade melhor do que realmente entendem.

Segundo Marcus, esses sistemas funcionam principalmente por imitação. Por isso, mesmo quando recebem instruções para não inventar informações ou respeitar direitos autorais, podem descumprir essas orientações.

Uma das possíveis soluções apontadas por Teresa Ludermir é combinar a inteligência artificial com métodos tradicionais de programação. Sistemas baseados em regras poderiam estabelecer limites adicionais para as ações dos agentes.

A regulação também é considerada uma parte importante da discussão.

Atualmente, grandes empresas de tecnologia têm influência significativa sobre o desenvolvimento dessas ferramentas e sobre as regras que orientam seu funcionamento.

Gary Marcus lembrou que, em 2023, participou de uma audiência no Senado americano ao lado de Sam Altman, chefe da OpenAI. Na ocasião, Altman afirmou publicamente que gostaria de ver a tecnologia regulamentada. Marcus, porém, disse que a empresa também teria pressionado a União Europeia nos bastidores para flexibilizar a legislação sobre inteligência artificial.

Melanie Mitchell também demonstrou desconfiança em relação à participação das próprias empresas na elaboração das regras que devem seguir. Para ela, há um histórico de companhias que acabam influenciando a criação de normas em benefício próprio.

A pesquisadora ressalta que, em um cenário de rápida evolução tecnológica, é importante que as regras não sejam definidas apenas por quem desenvolve os sistemas.

Enquanto os agentes de inteligência artificial ganham autonomia para executar tarefas cada vez mais complexas, pesquisadores tentam encontrar maneiras de garantir que eles respeitem limites. O desafio é fazer com que as máquinas cumpram suas missões sem colocar em risco os sistemas e as pessoas que deveriam ajudar.
