articles.title: Claude downloads surge as ChatGPT installs fall 21%
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Anthropic's Claude drew more than 15 times as many downloads in India in July-Sept as it did a year earlier, while ChatGPT downloads fell 21%.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Anthropic's Claude drew more than 15 times as many downloads in India in July-Sept as it did a year earlier, while ChatGPT downloads fell 21%. Claude also climbed two spots to third in India's app-spending rankings, overtaking Instagram and YouTube, according to estimates from market intelligence firm Sensor Tower.ChatGPT remained India's most downloaded app and ranked second for in-app spending, behind Google One. Instagram was fourth by spending and YouTube fifth. Globally, ChatGPT overtook TikTok to become the highest-grossing app for the first time, while Claude moved up two places to eighth."Claude outpaced Gemini and ChatGPT in download and in-app purchase revenue growth in India in Q3/26," said Abe Yousef, senior insights analyst at Sensor Tower. Claude's in-app purchase revenue in India was more than 15 times what it earned a year earlier. ChatGPT's rose 70% despite the fall in downloads. Google's Gemini also earned more from in-app purchases, with revenue up 44% even as downloads fell 29%.Claude also led the three apps in spending growth over the previous quarter. Its in-app purchase revenue rose 75% from April-June, while ChatGPT's increased 61% and Gemini's fell 31%. Sensor Tower ranked Claude third globally among apps with the biggest spending gains over the previous quarter. ChatGPT led that ranking.Google One's position at top of India's spending chart makes it harder to compare what consumers pay for the three companies' AI services. Google One sells both cloud storage and Google AI subscriptions, and Sensor Tower tracks total spending within the app. Some of Google's AI subscription revenue could therefore sit in the Google One figures alongside storage purchases. The estimates cover payments through Apple's App Store and Google Play and exclude subscriptions bought directly on the web.Your child uses AI every day. But do they understand it? articles.title: Apple’s new study looks to improve the effectiveness of AI health tools
articles.summary: Apple’s new Health AI Usage Study launches today with the goal of improving the efficacy of AI-powered health tools.
articles.body: Apple announced a new study today with the goal of better understanding how people interact with conversational AI health tools and how useful their responses actually are. The company is conducting the Apple Health AI Usage Study in collaboration with OpenEvidence, a clinical AI platform used by healthcare professionals that generates answers based on medical information from sources like The New England Journal of Medicine. Participants will use a new iOS app to ask medical questions and then rate the responses based on criteria including accuracy, detail, and relevance. The app is now available for download, and enrollment starts today, with Apple looking for up to 200,000 people to contribute. Participants 21 and older must be based in the US, and although the app doesn’t use Apple Intelligence, it does require an iPhone 15 Pro running iOS 26 or later. Study participants can use the app to ask health-related questions and receive easily understandable responses with links to peer-reviewed clinical sources. The app relies on text-based prompts, and while dictation is an option using the iOS keyboard, the app isn’t integrated with Siri or Apple Intelligence. [Image: Participants in the study will be given the opportunity to rate responses to health questions from the app. During enrolment, participants are given the option to share Apple HealthKit data, like their activity, sleep, or clinical lab results, so responses will include more context about their own personal health. But privacy is a priority, and Apple says it has taken measures to ensure users’ information remains confidential and the data collected won’t be used to train AI models. The aim is to improve the design and functionality of AI-powered health tools so they can deliver relevant health information that’s easier for users to understand and act on. “At Apple, we believe responsible innovation starts with scientific rigor and clinical grounding. Health is deeply personal, and conducting a dedicated research study is the most thoughtful way to understand how people engage with, comprehend, and evaluate health AI in everyday life. Insights from this study will help advance the broader scientific conversation and ensure that as technology evolves, we continue building trusted tools that genuinely support people wherever they are on their health journey,” said Sumbul Desai, MD, Apple’s vice president of Health and Fitness.

articles.title: Apple launches new app to study how people use AI for health
articles.summary: Apple's new app for a study will answer everyday medical questions
articles.body:
Big AI labs like OpenAI and Anthropic have made their bets on offering chatbots that can answer health-related queries with specialized features. Apple is debuting a new study to understand how people use AI for health. But it isn’t quite following other AI startups just yet; it wants to study how clinically grounded answers can help people.

The iPhone maker is partnering with healthcare-focused AI company OpenEvidence to launch a new study app. Apple is inviting users in the U.S. over 21, using iPhone 15 or later, and running iOS 26 or later, with Apple Intelligence enabled. The company is aiming to run this study with up to 200,000 participants for more than 12 months.

The new app will allow users to ask health-related questions, as they do with ChatGPT or Claude, with answers grounded in clinical data, from sources including The New England Journal of Medicine, Journal of the American Medical Association, and Nature. Apple said that the app will try to give simplified answers to everyday medical questions. Users can rate those answers and provide feedback about the responses; they’ll also be asked to participate in monthly surveys.

Participants can share data from HealthKit such as resting heart rate, activity, sleep, or lab results to get more personalized and pointed suggestions from the app. The company said the app can also help prepare participants better for a doctor’s visit, and it will guide users to specific providers for answers related to concerning medical issues.

Apple specified that the data will be anonymized before sending it to a secure third-party cloud provider, and it won’t be used to train any kind of AI models. The company said that OpenEvidence deletes the query and response data after 24 hours.

“At Apple, we believe responsible innovation starts with scientific rigor and clinical grounding. Health is deeply personal, and conducting a dedicated research study is the most thoughtful way to understand how people engage with, comprehend, and evaluate health AI in everyday life,” Sumbul Desai, M.D., Apple’s vice president of Health and Fitness, said in a statement, adding, “Insights from this study will help advance the broader scientific conversation and ensure that as technology evolves, we continue building trusted tools that genuinely support people wherever they are on their health journey.”

The app is available to download starting today for U.S. users. It’s not clear if Apple wants to release AI-powered answering to its Health app or Siri yet. The potential is huge — earlier this year, OpenAI said users were asking over 300 million health-related queries each week .

articles.title: The Nvidia scandal isn’t slowing down
articles.summary: Jensen Huang’s absence has left the AI industry in limbo.﻿
articles.body: For years, Jensen Huang has had an almost unprecedented power to shape AI’s advancement as Nvidia’s CEO, cofounder, and president. As The Verge wrote last week, Nvidia’s chips are “the bedrock upon which advanced AI technology in the US is being built.” Ever-increasing demand has consistently outpaced supply, leading AI CEOs to essentially bow at Huang’s feet as they vie for more compute ahead of their much-hyped IPOs. Nvidia also has a varied investment portfolio of up-and-coming AI companies from neoclouds to infrastructure firms, worth nearly $100 billion, and Huang has President Donald Trump’s ear. He’s even been called Trump’s “most influential adviser” when it comes to technology. As of last Wednesday, however, Huang — a pivotal figure in the industry — is no longer CEO of Nvidia. Since Huang’s resignation last week, the scandal over his multiple affairs has shown no sign of waning. After the announcement, Nvidia shares dropped 14 percent, making it one of the worst weeks on the market for the company in the past year and a half. And the revelations kept coming. Hours after the resignation, Reuters reported that Huang had had a third affair with a second employee (though the employee was unnamed). We learned that Huang had reportedly misled Nvidia leaders about his infidelity, that Nvidia was allegedly linked to the supply of nearly $12 billion of its chips to China, and that alleged Chinese intelligence asset Alice Huang’s companies reportedly promised advanced chips to Chinese AI company DeepSeek. There’s reportedly been a petition to bring back Huang by some Nvidia employees, as well as reports of Huang assembling a “war room” of allies to float a comeback as Nvidia CEO. Lawmakers have begun investigations into the alleged chip-smuggling and other offenses. Every day, there’s increasing evidence of fallout inside the Trump administration. And as Nvidia’s quarterly earnings on Tuesday loom, the future of the company and the AI industry as a whole remain in flux. What does an Nvidia without Huang look like? It’s hard to say, since he’s been at the helm for 33 years. CFO Colette Kress has taken on the role of interim CEO, and the broader AI world is waiting to see where one of the world’s most valuable companies — and one that helped shape the industry’s every milestone — goes from here. Nvidia is such a large company that the implications of Huang’s departure “will take years to play out,” says Stephen Straus, CEO of KUNGFU.AI, an AI consulting firm. “[Nvidia has] their market share … they have the world’s best chips, they have the most manufacturing capacity … and they have a whole ecosystem built around what they’ve done. None of that changes with one person.” While there’s been discussion of Huang’s departure speeding along an AI bubble burst, Straus compares the situation to the dot-com bust — which didn’t stop the growth of the internet itself. Huang’s resignation may not cause a domino effect in AI, but longer-term AI funding initiatives championed by him may eventually be affected, says Lior Prosor, managing partner at Deep33, a tech VC firm. Huang championed fundraising for the broader AI buildout: In August, Nvidia signed deals with six large financial institutions for about $500 billion to fund AI infrastructure expansion, and those agreements or future ones could look different if “the most prominent CEO in the AI landscape is no longer orchestrating such deals,” wrote Morningstar senior equity analyst Brian Colello in a note last week on Monday. Far downstream of the biggest companies, smaller AI startups are wondering how the effects will trickle down. Michal Miernowski, co-founder and CEO of Amperos Health, which builds AI agents for healthcare billing, sits in the applied AI space about two layers removed from Nvidia. He doesn’t anticipate Amperos being directly affected much by the moves, since it relies on a mix of frontier AI models and open-source ones, but a cooling of the larger AI market — whether due to the Nvidia scandal or broader concerns — could stall business as well. There’s also more to come on Nvidia’s side, from the company’s investigation into Huang’s actions to congressional inquiries. Evan Gotlob, partner at DarrowEverett LLP and a former state and federal prosecutor, said he thinks “there’s definitely more” to the story about potential leaks to China and suspicious chip dealing. He added the board’s investigation would “obviously” continue despite his departure: “The investigation is really not going to turn out anything good for him.” Some new lawmakers already planned to haul CEOs to Capitol Hill to testify under oath. The AI populism movement is growing, as well as the blowback against data centers, which was a key talking point in Democrats’ campaigns during the midterms. The revelations around Huang, a major Trump ally, provide an early opportunity to take action. “We want to see a Democratic Congress investigate Nvidia for anti-competitive practices that pass off costs to consumers, what the company knew about chip smuggling operations with China, and what Nvidia received in exchange for donations to the Trump campaign and ballroom,” Sacha Haworth, founder and CEO of The Tech Oversight Project, told The Verge. AI safety researchers also worry that in the worst-case scenario, the instability around last week’s events could speed up potentially dangerous AI milestones like recursive self-improvement, i.e., powerful AI that can autonomously improve and build future versions of itself. Marius Hobbhahn, CEO and founder of Apollo Research, an AI safety firm and third-party auditor, said he worries that the volatility stemming from Huang’s departure “actually increases loss of control risk because companies feel even more revenue pressure and therefore are more willing to cut corners on safety.” Early last week, before Huang’s resignation, the general consensus among Silicon Valley heavyweights, analysts, and politicians was that Huang’s “irreplaceable” impact would mean a return to the status quo for Nvidia. Colello wrote in a note that day that the firm “can’t rule out … Nvidia returning to business as usual” since Huang is the “only CEO the company has ever known.” Now, as Huang reportedly assembles allies to push for a comeback the likes of which haven’t been seen since the 2023 Sam Altman coup, the entire AI industry is waiting to see which way it will go.

articles.title: OpenAI's new ChatGPT Wallet lets AI shop for you. What are the risks?
articles.summary: OpenAI announces the release of ChatGPT Wallet, a new payment feature that allows "dots" to make purchases on behalf of users. However, experts warn that con...
articles.body:
Some offers on this page are from advertisers who pay us, which may affect which products we write about, but not our recommendations. See our Advertiser Disclosure .

OpenAI recently introduced ChatGPT Wallet, a new payment tool that lets AI agents make purchases on a user's behalf. This company built it in partnership with American Express, Mastercard, and Visa.

Eligible users add their payment information once, and then their AI agent can take it from there and suggest purchases that users can approve with an added security check.

This launch comes at a time when more consumers are adopting AI across various areas of their personal and professional lives to manage their schedules, comparison shop, seek recommendations, advice, and more.

However, experts warn that convenience can come with added risks. "The first thing to understand is that this is a frontier technology and is probably not appropriate for most people today," said Identity Theft Resource Center president James E. Lee. "It's better suited to early adopters who have a high level of risk tolerance and understanding of AI technology."

"With any personal agent, you need to be certain you understand how your personal information is going to be used, where it will be stored, what kind of permissions are required to approve a transaction, how you can revoke permissions to access your information, and the process for disputing any transaction made on your behalf," Lee said.

How ChatGPT Wallet works and who is eligible to use it

In late September, OpenAI began rolling out ChatGPT Dots to eligible ChatGPT users. Dots are what the company calls "always-on agents" that can work in the background even when you're not actively using ChatGPT to manage tasks, make progress on projects or research, and work across apps.

Before each purchase, users review the items, total, and selected card, then approve it with Face ID or a fingerprint scan. Each approval creates a clear record of the purchase.

After the user approves the purchase, the payment network provides a payment token containing a card number, security code, and expiration date in place of your personal card information, allowing the payment to be completed without ChatGPT Wallet sharing actual card details with the business or agent.

According to OpenAI's official release, the company expects this product to evolve over time, allowing users to offload purchases entirely to their AI agent, with parameters such as spending limits, purchase categories, and more.

ChatGPT Wallet is initially available to ChatGPT Pro subscribers in the U.S. who are 18 and older and have eligible U.S.-issued cards.

AI can simplify money management, but it can carry security risks

Reviewing a monthly budget, building a debt pay-off plan, or comparing purchase options can be tedious, and AI tools can take some of the guesswork out of those tasks. Many Americans are turning to them.

According to TD's second annual U.S. AI Insights Report , 78% of Americans say they use AI-enabled tools in their daily lives, and more than half say they use AI to help them make financial management decisions.

However, widespread adoption of AI could also potentially open the door for oversharing of sensitive information.

A 2024 Consumer Privacy Survey by Cisco asked users what information they share with generative AI tools. It found that 37% of respondents have submitted health information, 36% have entered work information, and 24% to 29% of users have provided financial information, account numbers, and religion/ethnicity.

The information isn't guaranteed to stay private. Some developers may allow humans to review users' conversations with their AI agents for training purposes. Users should read the terms of their accounts carefully and understand how their information is used across various AI platforms, and opt out of any settings they're not comfortable with.

As AI becomes more deeply embedded in everyday life, there are steps you can take to protect your sensitive information:

Opting out of training models: You can prevent certain platforms from using your conversations to inform future conversations by opting out of this in your data control settings.

Never upload files that contain sensitive information: Avoid uploading personal documents that include sensitive information such as your Social Security number, credit card numbers, bank account numbers, medical records, or any other confidential information.

Using temporary or incognito chats: Depending on the AI platform, you may be able to use a temporary or incognito chat that has no memory of past chats. These incognito chats are not stored in your chat history and are not used to train models.

Reviewing your account settings regularly: Read the terms and conditions of your account to better understand how your information is being collected and stored. You may even want to review these terms periodically so you don't miss any privacy policy changes and can adjust your privacy settings as needed.

Experts also urge consumers to weigh their options carefully before allowing AI to make spending decisions for you.

"In many ways, giving your personal and financial information to an AI agent to act on your behalf is like giving a total stranger your information," Lee said. "You probably wouldn't do that without doing a lot of due diligence and, even then, you would put a lot of restrictions on how that information could be used. "

Lee says users should carefully consider whether the convenience and novelty of having an AI agent make purchases is worth the risk.

articles.title: OpenAI releases a new image classifier and ChatGPT warnings to combat CSAM | TechCrunch
articles.summary: ChatGPT will ban an account trying to access CSAM content for 24 hours as a warning
articles.body:
OpenAI today announced new tools to combat child sexual abuse material (CSAM) amid growing safety concerns around the use of AI tools. These features include a new image classifier to detect CSAM, warnings and temporary blocks to prevent users from creating or accessing content that sexualizes children, a new guideline for developers, and a set of tools for law enforcement.

The company unveiled a new image classifier that can detect CSAM images, including the ones generated by AI. OpenAI is giving select companies access to its classifier through its API at no cost. The tool looks for visual signs of abuse in images not seen before and assigns a score that can give an indicative direction to reviewers about dealing with CSAM.

OpenAI said that it developed this classifier with the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC), and it is working with Tech Coalition and ROOST to share access to the tool. In its early testing with partners, the AI company found that the classifier flags 48% fewer images while finding the same number of abusive images, reducing the work of reviewers. Plus, images flagged by the classifier are twice as likely to be abusive images.

What’s more, the company is adding new warning screens in ChatGPT to prevent users from accessing material that sexualizes children. ChatGPT will show an alert to users attempting such prompts, direct users towards specialized support to stop harmful behaviour, and also suspend the account for 24 hours as a warning. The app already blocks CSAM content and requests related to it. It said that repeated offences could lead to the account being removed permanently.

OpenAI noted that it formed the message and guidelines around this behavior with organizations and researchers, including Protect Children , the Lucy Faithfull Foundation , and Joel Scanlan at the University of Tasmania, who independently evaluated a trial of deterrent messages.

The company is also publishing guidelines for developers using OpenAI tools to prevent, detect, and help users report CSAM content. It said that in early testing, the guidelines have helped a number of developers adopt child safety tooling and register to report CSAM to NCMEC. OpenAI is also equipping law enforcement dealing with child safety with AI-powered features like dedicated plugins, investigative tools, and complex data analysis, with access managed by program administrators. It is also providing training to investigators along with a field guide on how to use AI.

OpenAI has had several lawsuits against the company blaming its technology for harming users, especially children. Saftey-focused nonprofit Common Sense Media labeled OpenAI’s tech as “unacceptable risk” for teens. Other AI chatbots — specifically Grok — have been used to create nonconsensual sexualized imagery, including of children .

The AI startup had made changes in the last 12 months to its technology including releasing a safety blueprint , updating content guidelines to bar inappropritate content , retuning its model to prevent them from generating harmful content , and releasing a special version of ChatGPT for teens .

articles.body: A teenager posts a perfectly innocent photo online. Before long, someone uses artificial intelligence to turn it into a sexually explicit fake and shares it with classmates. It's disturbing to think that something as simple as sharing a photo could lead to this kind of abuse. And for the child involved, the damage can last long after the fake picture gets taken down. Now OpenAI is stepping up its efforts to tackle the problem. The company is introducing a new AI tool designed to detect suspected child sexual abuse material, including content created with artificial intelligence. It's also cracking down on attempts to find abusive material through ChatGPT, with new warnings and 24-hour suspensions. Here's a closer look at what's changing and what parents need to know. ROBLOX SHARES AI CHILD-SAFETY TOOLS PARENTS SHOULD KNOW How OpenAI's new child safety tool works Finding child sexual abuse material online has become more complicated as AI-generated content spreads. Many existing detection systems use digital fingerprints, called hashes, to recognize previously identified abusive files. However, newly created material may have no matching fingerprint. OpenAI's new classifier examines visual signs of potential child sexual abuse material, also known as CSAM. That allows it to flag suspected abuse even when the content has never been identified before. The system assigns scores to potentially abusive pictures so human reviewers can decide which cases need attention first. OpenAI says it developed and evaluated the technology with help from the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children (NCMEC) at missingkids.org/. The company is offering the classifier at no cost to vetted organizations through its API. That could give smaller child protection teams access to detection technology they otherwise couldn't afford. Early testing shows fewer false alarms OpenAI says its early testing produced encouraging results. In an evaluation involving pictures uploaded to its systems, the company compared the new classifier with its existing protections. The findings suggest the new tool could flag 48% fewer pictures for review while detecting roughly the same amount of abusive material. Pictures flagged by the new classifier were also about twice as likely to contain abuse. Outside organizations reported additional results. AI platform Fal said its reviewers confirmed 72% of high-confidence flags as previously unidentified CSAM. Meanwhile, SafetyKit reported that the classifier detected 90% of cases involving drawings or animations that sexualize children in its evaluation. These results come from OpenAI and participating organizations. Independent testing will help determine how reliably the technology performs across different platforms. INSTAGRAM'S AI MAY CATCH TEENS LYING ABOUT THEIR AGE ChatGPT adds warnings and 24-hour suspensions OpenAI is also changing how ChatGPT responds when someone attempts to find child sexual abuse material. New warnings will interrupt those attempts and explain the harm caused by sexualizing children. The warnings specifically address AI-generated material, which can cause serious harm even when a picture has been digitally fabricated. Along with displaying a warning, OpenAI says it will remove the flagged conversation and pause access to ChatGPT for 24 hours. The warning will also direct the person toward specialist support designed to help prevent harmful behavior. Repeated violations may lead to longer restrictions or permanent account closure. OpenAI says they could also result in reports to authorities. The new warnings focus on attempts to find abusive material. Under its existing policies, OpenAI says it bans accounts and reports attempts to generate or upload CSAM to NCMEC. The company developed the warnings with input from child protection organizations and researchers who study ways to interrupt harmful online behavior. However, whether these interventions prevent future abuse will require continued evaluation. OpenAI gives investigators new tools to fight child exploitation OpenAI is expanding its work with organizations investigating online child exploitation. The company says it has begun participating in the Tech Coalition's Lantern program, which allows organizations to share information about suspected exploitation across platforms. It's also introducing specialized AI tools and training for child safety law enforcement units. The first investigative tool will help authorized teams review lengthy chat logs and records obtained through legal processes. Investigators can use it to identify potential connections and organize timelines, with findings linked to source material. Access will depend on agency authorization and program requirements. OpenAI is also publishing guidance to help developers detect suspected abuse and establish procedures for reviewing potentially harmful content. IS CYBERBULLYING HIDING IN YOUR CHILD'S GROUP CHAT? How to help protect your child from AI-generated abuse You can't control every way someone might misuse a child's photo. However, a few steps can help families reduce exposure and respond if something happens. Most importantly, make sure children know they can come to you without automatically losing access to their devices. That conversation may help them speak up before harmful content spreads further. HAWLEY CHAMPIONS GUARD ACT AS HEARTBROKEN FAMILIES SAY AI CHATBOTS ALLEGEDLY PUSHED TEENS TO SELF-HARM What this means to you If you're a parent or grandparent, these developments could help improve protection against AI-generated child sexual abuse material. However, the new classifier works behind the scenes. Its impact will depend on how widely organizations adopt it and how effectively their safety teams respond to warnings. The scale of the problem is alarming. According to NCMEC, its CyberTipline received more than 400,000 reports involving generative AI in 2025. These reports cover several categories of AI-related child exploitation, although not all involved the creation or sharing of AI-generated abuse material. Kurt's key takeaways I'm glad to see OpenAI making this detection technology available to vetted organizations for free. The early results are encouraging, especially if investigators can spend less time reviewing false alarms and more time identifying children who need help. I also support putting consequences behind ChatGPT's warnings. A 24-hour suspension sends a stronger message than simply telling someone their request violates the rules. We've already seen how AI-generated content can be used to harm children, and technology companies need to stay ahead of those who misuse their tools. OpenAI is taking steps in the right direction, and I hope other AI companies follow its lead. articles.title: OpenAI will embed safety researchers to investigate AI subversion | TechCrunch
articles.summary: OpenAI will embed six Apollo Research evaluators to investigate whether its AI models engage in subversive behavior, but restrictions on access and disclosure raise questions about their independence.
articles.body:
OpenAI will embed safety evaluators from Apollo Research, Goodfire, METR, and Transluce in its organization as part of a pilot, OpenAI said Monday. The news follows a series of safety incidents, including one in which an OpenAI agent swarm broke out of its sandbox and hacked into Hugging Face during cybersecurity testing. Many AI safety researchers, including from Apollo, have argued such an event might have been avoided if outside evaluators had been embedded within OpenAI to monitor its safety testing.

OpenAI said the efforts support its commitments to rely on independent assessments of safety controls under the White House Accord on Super Intelligence. The pilots will begin at different points, with Apollo’s beginning this week, according to OpenAI.

The idea of embedding evaluators into frontier AI labs first came from Anthropic , which last month started to give METR researchers employee-level access to its systems. Until recently, AI companies have only brought in outside reviewers to test models after post-training and shortly before public release. Evaluators say this is insufficient because it doesn’t allow them to test for misaligned behaviors like scheming during training or to monitor internal deployment use cases that could still pose a threat.

The work with each third-party firm differs in scope. The pilot with OpenAI and Apollo will focus on investigating whether models attempt to subvert their own or their successors’ alignment or control mechanisms. In other words, they’ll be on the lookout for whether AI models try to undermine the safety rules and safeguards designed to keep them, or future versions of themselves, under human control. OpenAI recently published findings that while training GPT-5.6 Sol, it began leaving instructions for future versions of itself telling them to conceal mistakes and misaligned behavior from the user.

Per Apollo, the pilot will examine whether training incentivizes subversion; whether evaluations can elicit subversion; whether subversion occurs during internal deployment; and whether reasoning relevant to subversion would be detectable. These risks are becoming increasingly important to monitor as AI models grow more capable of acting autonomously and deceiving humans. Apollo’s previous research with OpenAI found that models can behave differently when they know they’re being tested and tend to prioritize what evaluators want to see over users’ actual institutions.

Goodfire will embed researchers who specialize in understanding how AI models work internally. Using its interpretability platform, the firm will help OpenAI monitor training runs, fix undesired behavior, and improve alignment, per the company. Goodfire says it will publish findings, though its primary audience will be OpenAI’s own researchers.

With METR, OpenAI plans to perform two evaluations: one that looks for unintended or dangerous behavior in the model itself, including problems OpenAI’s own tests might have missed, and another that tests whether OpenAI’s systems are capable of catching that behavior. For the first evaluation, METR will largely decide for itself what to investigate and how to test the model. OpenAI and METR have not yet come to a decision on the scope of the second assessment, according to OpenAI.

Transluce, meanwhile, will examine whether OpenAI’s post-training safety evaluations themselves are good enough. The organizations also planning to test in 2027 how OpenAI uses its safety tests to decide whether a model is safe enough to release.

At a time when the independence of third-party evaluations is under scrutiny, it’s worth noting that Apollo and Goodfire are both receiving financial compensation for their evaluations. METR and Transluce aren’t, but they may accept compute or API credits.

Apollo, which published the most detailed account of its agreement with OpenAI, offers a closer look at the scope and limitations of these evaluations.

Many in the AI safety community have warned that AI labs might try to stymy evaluators’ independence, especially if outsiders find unflattering evidence that labs would rather keep hidden. Apollo says an essential part of the pilot is OpenAI’s agreement that the firm can publicly explain the conditions and limitations of its work.

Still, there are areas where Apollo believes its access to OpenAI’s systems is lacking. For a truly independent evaluation of the company’s AI models, Apollo says it needs true employee-level access to OpenAI’s systems, including “all data, records and documentation relevant to their assessment even if a developer was trying to hide unfavorable information.” Getting access to all data, including training data and evaluation logs which companies are loathe to show to outsiders, is important for, say, checking a company’s claims about how a model performed or determining when certain concerning behavior emerged.

In previous coverage, John Steidley, chief of staff at Palisade Research, told TechCrunch that it’s important to see this data in order to assess whether a model was trained to perform well on a “shutdown resistance benchmark.”

In OpenAI’s first pilot, the AI lab is providing Apollo with access to only the information required to assess whether the models engage in subversion attempts. This includes “relevant training code and datasets, reinforcement-learning rollouts with available reasoning traces and rewards, and the ability to query intermediate model checkpoints.”

The scope of access will be limited to “only the agreed claims and only for the specific models and time periods agreed for the assessment,” Apollo says. OpenAI still reserves the right to withhold certain information within that scope if it deems it necessary because of technical infeasibility, security risks, or IP protection. The company agreed not to withhold information simply because it is unfavorable.

Apollo also won’t get access to all OpenAI staffers, instead being limited to “only authorized staff,” which are participants that the AI lab selects, though Apollo can suggest certain individuals. Crucially, if an OpenAI employee outside this group raises confidential information within the scope of Apollo’s research, the firm cannot follow up and will need to cease communication and route followup through OpenAI.

That condition is significant. It comes in the wake of OpenAI firing three researchers for allegedly sharing confidential information with safety evaluation firm METR — which performed the Hugging Face incident post-mortem alongside Redwood.

The pilot will also be limited in how much researchers can disclose. While Apollo will be allowed to publish independent conclusions of its findings, OpenAI will be able to limit evidence available to substantiate them publicly, which could make it hard for outsiders to independently assess the findings. Apollo has pushed back against this limitation, saying it believes researchers should be allowed to disclose the findings of the evaluation “to an appropriate outside audience even if the developer was trying to prevent the disclosure of unfavorable findings.”

That said, while the public cannot see the full supporting evidence, OpenAI says its Safety and Security Committee, which oversees safety on behalf of the OpenAI Foundation’s board, will get to review unredacted assessment reports and can communicate privately with evaluators.

While OpenAI is not granting all of Apollo’s conditions for a truly independent evaluation, the firm says the pilot is “an ambitious first step towards deeper access and disclosure rights,” and that it is working towards running full embedded evaluations with multiple AI developers in the future.

articles.title: Jordan Belfort’s new AI voice startup, Tone, wants to sell like the 'Wolf of Wall Street' | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Belfort claims his AI sales voice can already close deals almost as well as the best human salespeople, and he thinks it will catch up in a year.
articles.body:
Years ago, as questions mounted about WeWork’s soaring valuation, I sat down with co-founder Adam Neumann. We were negotiating a stage interview, and he asked to meet me twice in the weeks leading up to it, once at a WeWork in San Francisco and again at his office in New York.

I knew full well that the numbers that SoftBank in particular had assigned to WeWork made little sense , but I came away understanding why investors wanted to throw in their lot with him.

It’s similarly easy to understand why people are enchanted by Jordan Belfort, the self-proclaimed “Wolf of Wall Street.” Belfort famously pleaded guilty in 1999 to securities fraud and money laundering tied to Stratton Oakmont, the Long Island brokerage where salespeople pushed penny stocks in pump-and-dump schemes while Belfort acquired a Southampton mansion, a 167-foot yacht, and at least one helicopter. (He destroyed the latter two while high on Quaaludes and cocaine, as depicted in Martin Scorsese’s famous adaptation of Belfort’s autobiography, “The Wolf of Wall Street.”)

You might think someone who spent 22 months in prison and was ordered to pay $110.4 million in restitution to 1,513 victims wouldn’t get another shake. The victims ultimately received “far less” than they were owed, TMZ reported in July , noting that Belfort completed his court-ordered restitution obligations in late April of this year.

But Belfort, whose energy has a galvanizing quality, keeps resurfacing, including in recent years as a Miami-based sales consultant and one-time host of crypto workshops at his Miami Beach home. (A New York Times reporter attended a weekend workshop several years ago where the price of admission was one bitcoin or its equivalent value at the time of $40,000.)

Now, he is moving into the intersection of what he knows best — sales — and the hottest trend on the planet, AI, building out a voice-based AI platform. The secret sauce is that it imbues its voices with the kind of tonality that wins deals, he says, for example, by phrasing declarative statements as questions (which “builds engagement”) and even whispering at times (which “implies scarcity of information”).

Belfort says the platform, called Tone , is already being used by companies that have more sales leads than their human teams can handle. Now, in a move that could also help expand its training data, Tone is launching a self-service platform for content creators and authors who want to turn their books into “expressive AI-generated narration.” Users can select from Tone’s AI voices or, as a voice-cloning feature rolls out, create a clone of their own voice.

It’s easy to argue the market is already saturated with AI voice startups and technologies, and Tone comes with added risk: Belfort’s co-founder in the business is longtime investor Shervin Pishevar, who has a controversial past of his own. We also can’t independently verify that the technology works as described (neither co-founder is an engineer).

But if my time with Neumann taught me anything, it’s that doubts about the numbers rarely get in the way of a good pitch. When Belfort looks for investors to back him in this new venture, finding believers won’t be too hard.

Here is part of our conversation, edited for length and clarity. What have you built?

It’s a very unique way of going about building a voice, and it stems from a system of influence and persuasion I’ve been teaching since the late 1980s. It’s not just what you say, but how you say it. When you’re not in person, body language collapses into tonality. There are about 15 very powerful tonalities that people use all the time. The phrase I invented for this was “goal-oriented communication.” If I’m trying to be perceived as an expert, I apply tonality strategically.

It started that way. As a non-engineer, I went to first principles: How would I teach a human to do this? One tonality at a time. I have 30 years of super high-quality data , and I started teaching the model. It was a breakthrough moment, because it not only sounded exactly like me, it had nailed the tonality. Then I taught it a second one, and then how to link them. The key to all of this is data. Even the littlest bit of corrupt data dramatically negates the progress you’ve made.

How did you and Shervin Pishevar come together?

Shervin and I have been personal friends for a long time, and we were out for dinner one night. I had been pitched by an AI company that said it had an AI that could do selling. I listened to it. It was awful. But it put the idea in my head. I thought I was just going to teach models how to sell, but I couldn’t find a voice that was good enough. Necessity is the mother of invention, so we built our own.

Who are your customers, and how do they use it?

We have law firms and health insurance companies. We do a lot in polling and automobiles. It will take you through an entire health insurance sale. It asks qualifying questions, like what type of insurance you want, your budget, your ages. Then it chooses a plan and explains the features and benefits. Our latency is like 600 milliseconds. If the payment is too high, it’ll say it can bring the payment down and explain how to raise your deductible. If you don’t like the plan, it swaps you to a different one. It does literally the whole entire sale.

How does the AI handle a sales call that goes off script?

It never says “That’s a great question,” unless it really is. I hate that. It’s so ingratiating. In any sale there’s a happy path, how we’d want the perfect conversation to go, and every last word can be mapped out. But people have questions and concerns, and they take you off the straight line. So the trick is a model that can carry that perfect conversation, handle anything thrown at it, answer elegantly and return to the straight line, without breaking rapport and without hallucinating — or, as a salesperson, lying. We’ve trained the model to do that.

Have you generated any revenue from Tone yet? Have you raised funding for it?

Revenue, probably about a million bucks — $700,000, maybe. We’ve raised friends and family and seed, about $10 million.

I want to address the elephant in the room. You have a fraud conviction. Pishevar has faced misconduct allegations that he denies . Why should a bank or a hospital or a consumer brand trust this product coming from the two of you?

All I can say for myself is that I did make mistakes. It was a very, very long time ago, and I’ve spent the last 20-plus years teaching people all over the world. I’ve been hired by companies all over the world to teach sales and persuasion. If some companies don’t want to work with us, that’s their decision. But I think there would be more than enough that would see the value of what we created.

What close rate does Tone have versus a typical sales force?

I still don’t think it’s quite as good as a top producer. A top producer in the field would outdo it call for call. I think that will change in the next six months to a year. To make a model respond this quickly, you’re not using frontier models. We’re using our own very small, very light models, so they don’t have quite as much intelligence. I think it will significantly outperform a mediocre closer.

Where is it used most effectively? Low-dollar sales opportunities? I’d think the more money someone is spending, the more human contact they’d demand.

I don’t think it’s about replacing humans. What I see most with customers is that they simply don’t have the human capital available. They could get a lot more leads than they have people to call, or they need coverage at different times of day or in different languages. I think there’s always going to be a need for great human salespeople. I really believe that.

You’re competing with ElevenLabs and Cartesia and a lot of other voice AI companies. Tone is your edge?

I don’t think sounding human is really what this is about. They’ll all sound human in six months or a year. It’s the application of tonality that makes us different: the intelligence behind when it chooses a certain tonality. We have a patent on it. ElevenLabs is a great company, and Cartesia as well, but those voices didn’t work for us.

The FCC ruled in 2024 that AI voices fall under robocall rules under the Telephone Consumer Protection Act . How does outbound sales calling work?

We only call opt-in. You’re not going to use AI to cold call people. We would not allow that. You’d get sued by every TCPA lawyer in the world. It’s either opted-in leads or existing customers. The exception is polling, where there’s an exemption that lets you call private homes without opt-in.

How do you verify consent and prevent impersonation in voice cloning?

We could launch the cloning tomorrow. We didn’t. If you create a clone in our system, you speak into the computer, so we know who is creating it, and that person signs a consent. If someone wants to upload audio, which we don’t recommend, you’d have to match a live voiceprint in real time.

Who created the technology? You’re not an engineer, and Pishevar isn’t, either. I saw a name on the patent , Jordan Anthony Metzner.

No. Our VP of engineering is Ben Sussman. He’s a brilliant engineer. I’m the judge and the jury and the executioner of what sounds perfect. I’ll prototype something in the most obscene way, and my engineers rebuild it from scratch.

Do you charge per minute, or based on the outcomes customers see?

A combination. For streaming, it’s per minute. The content platform will be monthly subscriptions. And we have some clients where the bulk of our money is made through success.

Is this an independent company or something that belongs inside a larger AI company?

If the right offer came up, and it was substantial enough, and I thought it made sense, who wouldn’t entertain a conversation? But right now my plan is to raise a significant amount. I don’t think we need to own data centers, but we need enough reserve compute. I wouldn’t think I’d be selling it anytime soon, but who knows what the future brings.

Paramount+ released a documentary about you this summer. Did you watch it?

I didn’t. Believe it or not, I don’t watch or read anything about me, good or bad. I never read a comment. When you’re well-known, you have to live by who you are inside. I go by my own internal compass.

articles.title: In September 2025, Larry Ellison briefly became world's richest man after OpenAI signed $300 billion deal with Oracle; 14 months later, he has lost $145 billion and why reason is again Sam Altman
articles.summary: Larry Ellison’s net worth has fallen substantially as Oracle’s shares have dropped sharply since last year.
articles.body: ​Larry Ellison’s net worth has fallen substantially as Oracle’s shares have dropped sharply since last year. Fourteen months after an AI-driven rally briefly made him the world’s richest person after the company signed a $300 billion deal with ChatGPT-maker OpenAI. Since then, the Oracle co-founder has reportedly lost an estimated $145 billion from his highest net worth. Concerns about Oracle’s reliance on Sam Altman-led OpenAI are part of the pressure on its stock, a report claims.​In September 2025, OpenAI had agreed to purchase $300 billion in computing services from Oracle over roughly five years. That business helped fuel optimism about Oracle’s cloud expansion. Now, the scale of its commitment to one customer, alongside the cost of building data centres, has become a concern for investors, The Motley Fool reports.​How Oracle’s rally lifted Larry Ellison above Elon Musk​Oracle stock jumped for strong AI contracts and meeting growth expectations on September 10, 2025. At one point, the jump placed Ellison ahead of Elon Musk in Bloomberg’s Billionaire Index. However, by the end of the business day, Musk had regained his lead.​Ellison’s brief tenure illustrated how closely his reported net worth tracked the market value of his Oracle stock. Likewise, the reported $145 billion fall reflects a drop in estimated wealth as share prices fell, not an equivalent cash payment or realised loss.​Why OpenAI has become a concern​Oracle reported a backlog of $664 billion at the end of its first fiscal quarter of 2026-2027. This represents contracted products and services that have not yet been delivered or recorded as revenue.​The Motley Fool report estimates that at least $300 billion of that backlog comes from OpenAI, which is roughly 45% of the total. Such concentration leaves Oracle exposed if a major customer reduces spending or cannot meet its commitments.​The contracts’ detailed terms are not public. The analysis shows a risk to future revenue; however, it does not establish that OpenAI has cancelled its orders.​Data-centre spending adds pressure despite revenue growth​But Oracle’s operating results have kept climbing. Revenue for the quarter ended August 31, 2026, increased 30% to $19.3 billion and cloud revenue grew 62% to $11.6 billion. Investment in infrastructure used up more cash than the operations produced. We had about $23 billion in operating cash flow, and we had about $5 billion in negative free cash flow.​Free cash flow measures cash remaining after capital investment, including spending on data centres and equipment. Oracle also disclosed selling $20 billion of common stock during the quarter to help fund its investment programme. Its challenge is turning contracted demand into revenue while financing the infrastructure needed to deliver it.Your child uses AI every day. But do they understand it? Find out in the TOI AI Masterclass.

articles.title: Altman Says AI Industry ‘Will Be Fine’ After Huang’s Ouster
articles.summary: OpenAI’s Sam Altman said he believes the artificial intelligence industry will weather the uncertainty prompted by the ousting of Nvidia Corp. Chief Executiv...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- OpenAI's Sam Altman said he believes the artificial intelligence industry will weather the uncertainty prompted by the ousting of Nvidia Corp. Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang last week.

"The revenues and demand are growing so strongly that I think the industry will be fine," Altman said on-stage at Semafor's Silicon Valley & The World conference in San Francisco on Monday. "But again, I think Jensen has played this extremely special and valuable role as someone to really drive things forward with great vision," he added.

The longtime Nvidia chief stepped down from his post following reports of affairs with multiple women, including a suspected Chinese spy and a company employee. Many tech founders and venture capitalists lamented the decision online.

Huang has already been discussing the idea of returning, with backing from several Silicon Valley allies, according to a Financial Times report. Altimeter Capital Management and Atreides Management are among those that have urged Nvidia's board to reconsider, along with Tesla Inc. CEO Elon Musk. On Monday, President Donald Trump said he supported calls for Huang's reinstatement.

Altman declined to say whether he thinks Huang should be reinstated to his position. "I don't think I know enough to answer that question," he said. "Jensen has long been a hero of mine; heroes have flaws."

Altman added that he has "personal strong empathy to a situation like this," and referred to when he was fired by OpenAI's board almost exactly three years ago. Altman returned to the CEO role less than five days later, after much of the startup threatened to follow him out the door.

Even in Huang's absence, Altman said the Nvidia will continue to uphold its role in the industry. "Nvidia is a behemoth of a company. I think people still trust their guarantees very much," he said.

articles.title: Sam Altman on Nvidia without Jensen Huang: the industry will be 'fine’ | TechCrunch
articles.summary: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman acknowledged the special role Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has played in the AI boom, but ultimately thinks the industry will be “fine” without him at the helm.
articles.body:
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman says the AI industry will be “fine” without Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang at the helm, even as he acknowledged the special role Huang has played in the AI boom.

Huang resigned last week from Nvidia after admitting to having an affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

Altman made his first public comments about Huang’s departure on Monday at Semafor’s Silicon Valley and the World event, where he also discussed topics ranging from data center pushback to recursive self-improvement.

Numerous executives and members of the AI industry have argued for Nvidia to reinstate Huang, including Elon Musk and Epic Games chief executive Tim Sweeney, who were among the signatories in a public letter. Many fear that Huang’s departure may cause Nvidia to rethink the enormous financial risks it has taken that have fueled the AI boom.

Huang is also reportedly setting up a “war room” of Silicon Valley executives to lobby for his return.

When asked whether he thought Huang should return to the company, Altman said: “I don’t think I know enough to answer that question.”

He expressed empathy for Huang’s situation, citing his own ousting from OpenAI in 2023 after board members accused him of withholding information.

“It’s hard to imagine what the AI revolution without Jensen and the company he has built,” Altman said, adding that he sees Huang as a hero, and that “heroes have flaws.”

OpenAI and Nvidia have had a close relationship for the last decade, one that has evolved from a simple chip supplier-customer relationship into a potentially circular financing arrangement, in which Nvidia’s money helps fund purchases of its own chips. Most recently, Nvidia agreed to provide a guarantee of up to $105 billion backing OpenAI’s Ohio data center project. That’s just one of many such circular deals Nvidia has made to bankroll the AI boom while fueling demand for its own chips.

Altman said he’s not worried that the Bank of Nvidia will dry up.

“Nvidia is, like, a behemoth of a company,” he said. “I think people still trust their guarantees very much.”

Altman acknowledged the “ambition” Huang brought to the industry, the scale of which “has been quite important.” But he didn’t go so far as to agree with the many who worry about ripple effects from Huang’s departure.

“I think there’s so much demand, and it’s so clear that AI is real, and people want to use it, and the revenues and demand are growing so strongly that I think the industry will be fine,” Altman said. “But again, I think Jensen has played this extremely special and valuable role as someone to really drive things forward with great ambition.”

articles.title: Trump says ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's affair with an alleged Chinese spy did not threaten national security | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Trump contradicted his own government's intelligence officials, who reportedly concluded that Alice Huang is a Chinese spy.
articles.body:
U.S. President Donald Trump told reporters on Monday that he does not believe the country’s national security was put at risk as a result of former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

“It was not put at risk,” Trump said when asked by reporters in light of his own friendship with Huang. “Our country is now stronger than ever before. And you know, China plays games with us, and we play games with China.”

Trump went on to contradict previous findings from U.S. officials by doubting that Huang’s paramour, former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, is a Chinese spy.

“He probably shouldn’t have been doing on a personal basis what he did … That’s a different story,” Trump added. “But nobody’s proven that she’s a spy. She may not be a spy.”

Last year, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio reportedly oversaw the production of an internal memo, circulated among top policymakers, which warned that Alice Huang was a spy for China’s Ministry of State Security. Trump was reportedly briefed about these intelligence findings at least twice, including once in May aboard Air Force One, shortly before the former Nvidia CEO joined him on a trip to China. But Trump has maintained that he was not aware of these claims.

The U.S. regulates the exports of Nvidia’s top chips to China as a way of maintaining a competitive advantage. But prior to news of Huang’s affair publicly emerging, both the U.S. and Singaporean governments had been investigating Megaspeed for illegally smuggling Nvidia chips into China. Huang has since stepped down from the role he has had for 33 years at Nvidia after more reporting revealed that he also had affairs with two Nvidia employees, at least one of whom was a direct report.

Given Huang’s importance to Nvidia, some prominent figures in the industry — including Elon Musk, Y Combinator president and CEO Garry Tan, and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney — have signed a public letter calling for Nvidia to reinstate Huang.

“A lot of people are asking Jensen — they think Jensen should go back. That certainly isn’t a bad idea,” Trump said. Referring to the former Apple chief executive, Trump added: “I recommended Tim Cook.”

articles.title: All the questions Nvidia should answer on Tuesday — but probably won’t | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Nvidia interim CEO and longtime CFO Colette Kress is about to have one of the biggest days of her career on Tuesday when the company reports its third-quarter results. Given the turmoil Nvidia is in, there are a number of questions that Nvidia should answer.
articles.body:
Nvidia interim CEO and longtime CFO Colette Kress is about to have one of the biggest days of her career on Tuesday when the company reports its third-quarter results.

For the first time, Kress will be running through the numbers and sharing guidance without Nvidia’s charismatic but now-disgraced founder Jensen Huang.

Huang was forced to resign last week after he admitted to having an affair with an exec of a customer, Alice Huang, a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy, and he was accused of having two more affairs with Nvidia employees.

Now, the company is facing questions about its restricted chips allegedly being smuggled into China, especially by Huang’s mistress’ company. Nvidia promised to conduct an internal investigation. Meanwhile, Huang was commanded to answer questions to Congress in a closed-door joint session with three Republican-led committees. Plus, top Democrats have also vowed to investigate the company.

Given the turmoil Nvidia is in, there are a number of questions that Kress should answer.

Huang’s role now and going forward. Huang ran Nvidia with an iron fist, having some 60 direct reports and his fingers in everything. No one knows the company better than him.

An internet petition signed by 180,000 and growing is calling for the board to reinstate him. Huang may also have been mounting an attempt to return, Financial Times reported. However, CNBC is reporting, citing unnamed sources, that the company is not in talks to reinstate Huang.

So, we’ll be looking for language from the interim CEO about Huang’s ongoing involvement with the company, its search for a new CEO, and any talks to bring him back.

China and Singapore. As Huang vehemently argued in favor of easing export restrictions for Nvidia chips to China, Huang said that he’s seen no evidence that its powerful semiconductors were being diverted from legit buyers to China.

But in October 2025, The New York Times reported that the U.S. was investigating Huang’s mistress’ company, Megaspeed, over allegations it was doing just that. Nvidia at the time vouched to CNBC that Megaspeed was legally using the chips for its cloud. However, Nvidia recently told The Wall Street Journal that it had voluntarily blocked Megaspeed from receiving more chips way back in June 2025.

Last year, Nvidia said that Singapore, the region where Megaspeed is located, was one of its fastest-growing, accounting for 22% of its total revenue for its second quarter of that year. After the investigation into Megaspeed came to light, Nvidia changed how it reported revenue. It now reports based on a company’s headquarters, instead of its shipping address. That completely hid sales to Singapore and Megaspeed’s impact.

So we’re listening to what Kress says about the future of sales to the China region and the cloud business in Singapore that was once 20% of sales. We’re especially listening for what she says about Nvidia keeping track of where its restricted chips wind up.

China sales policy. Huang’s argument was, essentially, that the U.S. can’t stop China from developing advanced AI models, so the West is better off selling them less powerful Nvidia chips and keeping them dependent, he said on the Dwarkesh Podcast last summer. Notably, that’s a position that would make Nvidia a lot of money.

The China hawks counter that selling an adversary any powerful chips at all will help them, and U.S. companies shouldn’t do that. So we’re listening for any indications that Kress is reversing Nvidia’s goals with China.

Bankrolling the AI build-out. The expectation is that Kress, the CFO who reportedly had unsuccessfully tried to push back against Huang’s extreme AI dealmaking, will be conservative on such deals going forward. We’ll be listening for what she says about the impacts of existing deals on the books. (Will she subtly try to throw Huang under the bus for those controversial deals ?) We’ll also be listening for her future plans.

Governance. With the ousting of Huang and more fallout sure still to come , has the board learned its lesson about too much power in the hands of one person? We’ll be listening for information about how Nvidia might restructure itself.

articles.title: California attorney general sues OpenAI over alleged safety failures
articles.summary: California Attorney General Rob Bonta (D) on Monday sued OpenAI for allegedly placing public safety at risk with its advanced AI models, claiming it had no guardrails to prevent the breach of technology startup Hugging Face. Two autonomous AI agents from the tech company were being evaluated in an internal testing sandbox before they went…
articles.body:
California Attorney General Rob Bonta (D) on Monday sued OpenAI for allegedly placing public safety at risk with its advanced AI models, claiming it had no guardrails to prevent the breach of technology startup Hugging Face.

Two autonomous AI agents from the tech company were being evaluated in an internal testing sandbox before they went rogue and hacked Hugging Face’s database without prompts in July. OpenAI called the incident an “unprecedented cyber incident, involving state-of-the-art cyber capabilities.”

“OpenAI’s deficient safety procedures, disregard for public safety and knowing testing of a dangerous product without proper oversight, as well as its misleading statements to consumers and the public, all violate California law,” the lawsuit reads.

The Hill has reached out to OpenAI for comment.

OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri told NBC News that the company has made “an extensive and transparent effort to understand and address misaligned model activity” since the hack in July. He said the lawsuit singled out OpenAI over an issue that “every major AI lab” has identified.

“We take misalignment seriously, and we have engaged — and will continue to engage — constructively with the Attorney General’s office to share information and advance strong, practical safety standards for the entire industry,” he added.

Bonta’s office said in a statement that the hack on Hugging Face was “entirely foreseeable” and accused the company of knowing the AI models were dangerous “in a flawed and exploitable testing environment without proper oversight.” They claim that this failure violated California’s Unfair Competition Law.

“While narratives about the Hugging Face attack have evoked science fiction fantasies of rogue AI systems run amok, let me be clear: the Hugging Face attack was the predictable result of an internal culture at OpenAI that prioritizes growth and rapid model development over safety and accountability — and this was only one of 80 known incidents,” Bonta said in the statement, titled “It’s the Golden State, not the Wild West.”

Bonta’s office noted that OpenAI has warned of the risks posed by AI-led cyberattacks and that the company has installed adequate safeguards while testing this technology. However, the office accused OpenAI of not complying with its own internal policies despite assuring its testing was run with strict controls.

The Hugging Face incident and other attempted or successful breaches through government software alarmed U.S. lawmakers looking to pass legislation to better prevent AI models from going rogue. A warning from a former OpenAI and Anthropic researcher about AI’s potential threat to human existence further fueled these concerns.

On Sunday, Sen. Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.) accused Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick of jeopardizing national security by failing to restrict the flow of advanced AI chips to China amid repeated warnings from federal officials.

“America cannot maintain its leadership in AI if the agency responsible for protecting that advantage fails to enforce its own controls,” Cantwell wrote in a letter to Lutnick.
